A new technology has been developed that integrates a Lyman-alpha filter with a standard photometer to enable precise U-band photometry in space-based and ground-based telescopes, excluding cosmic ray events. This innovation has been successfully demonstrated with the ZTF22 telescope, resulting in highly accurate U-band filters by reducing shot noise. The technique is based on the principle that Ly-alpha emission is only produced by interstellar space at a low rate, less than 0.2 events per second, providing a highly reliable cosmic ray exclusion method. The optical design of the filter is crucial in maintaining this exclusion rate, regardless of the telescope's collection area, by minimizing scattered light. The underlying physics of the technique and its underlying principles are explored in this research. Additionally, a potential space-based telescope application is highlighted, involving a simple, low-cost Ly-alpha filter photometer for addressing a key astrophysical puzzle: the puzzling UV brightness of blue galaxies observed at great cosmic distances. If successfully implemented, this mode would enable the most extensive, contiguous mapping of extragalactic space ever conducted, revealing crucial galaxy evolution data. The technological advancements described could also facilitate the creation of a large area UV space telescope, potentially a 6 meter diameter space-based facility, for answering similar fundamental questions. The cost-effectiveness and ease of implementing this technology make it an attractive solution for addressing a range of essential astrophysical research initiatives. The underlying code for this research has been made public, enabling others to use the Ly-alpha filter photometry technique in various applications. The specific code used to analyze the ZTF22 data is included in this research for public access, as well as an associated Python package for performing Ly-alpha filter photometry, which is available on the GitHub repository 'LymanPhotometry' for public use. The research code by J. M. Deusz has yielded 250 million useful U-band images in a 2 year period, as well as providing explicit cosmic ray occurrence at a rate of <0.2 event/second, demonstrating the Ly-alpha filter cosmic ray exclusion technique to be highly reliable. The research code provides explicit values of systematics by demonstrating that the Ly-alpha filter photometer has a mean shot noise of 0.03 mag when operating at its full collection area, as well as indicating an upper systematics bound based on a saturation event, as reported in this research and provided as public domain code for potential future applications. The research code provides an associated dataset that includes the actual images taken by the ZTF22 telescope using the Ly-alpha filter

In various information network applications, the overall system behavior should align with a predetermined reference system trait. The study of distributed control strategies for multi-agent systems, where agents are interconnected by directed networks, focuses on designing a collective control that maintains network invariance and achieves stability. It is shown that a specific distributed control approach, based on an ideal control strategy combined with a graph filter, is able to achieve both stability and invariance under a certain condition related to the network's communication graph. Furthermore, a decentralized filter design is presented, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations. Additionally, a broader application of this approach is demonstrated through a leader-following example, where a reference agent with limited system access can influence the system's trajectory. The ideal control strategy offers a flexible framework for achieving this by mapping the system's trajectory to a predetermined reference system state. Lastly, a formal method is derived for determining whether a given network configuration allows for an entirely stable and invariance-compliant solution. The method highlights that a necessary condition for achieving invariance is that the network's communication graph must be strongly connected. The study presents a scalable, distributed solution for mapping the system's trajectory to a predetermined reference system trait, allowing for global stability and invariance without the need for a centralized controller. The proposed approach has a lower computational complexity, as it only needs to perform a single iteration per time step, close to the efficiency of individual agent processing, making it suitable for a wide variety of network applications. The study also provides a general framework for the design of distributed ideal control strategies, offering a versatile tool for achieving system invariance. The approach can be applied to various real-world network applications by selecting an appropriate graph filter based on the specific requirements of the system trait in question. For instance, the study demonstrates that a distributed control strategy based on an ideal control approach combined with a Laplacian filter is able to achieve both stability and invariance in systems with tree-like networks, while systems with cyclic properties require an alternative filter approach, as demonstrated in a comparison of filter designs. The study presents a distributed ideal control strategy for autonomous systems, where the overall system behavior should align with a predetermined reference system trait. It is shown that a specific distributed control approach, based on an ideal control strategy combined with a graph filter, is able to achieve both stability and invariance under a certain condition related to the network's communication graph. The ideal control strategy offers a flexible framework for achieving this, as it can be mapped to a predetermined reference system state

We examine the creation of feature vectors for static and moving images within a time-based sequence. Image characteristics are represented by vectors which combine texture, color, and shape features, weighing them equally for consistency. However, our approach differs from traditional methods by tying each frame's feature vector to its relative time within the sequence. This enables seamless integration of new frames, even as the sequence grows or shrinks. By indexing images based on their similarity to previous frames, we can locate similar images within a database. To optimize processing, we take advantage of the hierarchical structure of image characteristics, using a coarse-to-fine method that starts with the highest level of detail when searching for similar images. This technique has a range of applications, including automatic image categorization and retrieval, as demonstrated through its implementation in a mobile image application for automatically indexing and tagging photos and videos across a continuous timeline. This optimization addresses the insensitivity to minor image differences by narrowing the search area and focusing only on the most relevant image characteristics. Furthermore, we highlight the potential risks of inaccurate indexing, such as misclassifying a human face as an animal due to a distracting background figure. While these errors can be reduced through improved image characteristics and prioritization of the most relevant features, our approach remains susceptible to these limitations. Finally, we expand our technique beyond static images to include video analysis, allowing the creation of a video index that automatically categorizes and tags clips within a continuous timeline. This index can be applied to various applications, including a mobile video surveillance system. Video characteristics are represented by vectors which combine motion, texture, color, and shape features, as well as audio and speech elements, with equal weighting for consistency. Similar to static images, our approach differs from traditional methods by tying each clip's feature vector to its relative time within the sequence. This enables seamless integration of new clips, even as the sequence grows or shrinks. By indexing videos based on their similarity to previous clips, we can locate similar videos within a database. To optimize processing, we take advantage of the hierarchical structure of video characteristics, using a coarse-to-fine method that starts with the highest level of detail when searching for similar videos. This technique has a range of applications, including automatic video categorization and retrieval. By combining static and moving image analysis, we can create a comprehensive picture index. This index can be applied to various mobile applications, including a photo and video management system that automatically indexes and tags clips across a continuous timeline. To optimize processing, we take advantage of the hierarchical structure of image and video characteristics

Physical keyless authentication protocols aim to securely verify the identity of entities without relying on shared secrets. A novel practical approach, called Spin & Verify, is grounded in quantum mechanics' no-cloning theorem. We explore the fundamentals of noiseless keyless authentication within idealized Gaussian channels. We introduce Kraussian channels as a viable representation of noisy channels and develop the no-cloning theorem's application to random variables. We establish two essential criteria for noiseless keyless authentication based on these variable representations. We demonstrate that the Spin & Verify protocol corresponds to achieving these criteria in an alternating sequence. We also identify the necessary conditions for noiseless keyless authentication in any arbitrary Gaussian channel, as well as in memoryless Gaussian channels. Furthermore, we discuss how these principles of no-cloning theorem-based keyless authentication can be realized in practical contexts. We have successfully applied these principles to develop the Spin & Verify protocol, which is demonstrated to outperform physical keyless protocols in terms of achieving secure authentication with reduced randomness. Additionally, we have adapted and modified the spin & verify concept to address multi-party authentication in a joint research paper. We investigate the movement of a particle over a wavy energy landscape, focusing on the wavy potential $V(q) = K\cos(2\pi q)$, for both its smooth and gritty variants. In the smooth case, the particle's motion is predicted to exhibit uniform transportation, with an average velocity directly proportional to $K$. In contrast, the gritty variant $V(q) = K\cos^2(2\pi q) $ displays different behavior and is solved using adiabatic invariant methods, revealing an average velocity in direct proportion to the square root of $K$. We demonstrate that this gritty potential can be mapped onto a purely washboard model, providing insights into the transition from smooth to gritty dynamics. Notably, this transition is marked by a shift from first-order to second-order viscous behavior, as characterized by the exponent $\alpha = 1$ for $K^1$ and $\alpha = 2$ for $K^{1/2}$ respectively. Furthermore, our research reveals the existence of a transitional phase between these two states, where the particle exhibits uniform transportation for intermediate $K$ values. We develop a theoretical framework for this transitional phase and verify its correctness using numerical simulations in the effective model. In addition, we draw a parallel between our findings and recent experiments on washboard-like surfaces, discussing the implications of our results in the process. Last but not least, we make a prediction about the range of parameters in which uniform transportation occurs in the negative wavy potential $V(q) = -K\cos(2\pi q)$. In this prediction, we also connect our results to recent experiments on negative wavy surfaces. Through this study, we expand the boundaries of uniform transportation, offering insights into the complex and intriguing phases of particle dynamics on wavy energy landscapes. Lastly, we leave a prediction about the range of parameters in uniform transportation for the negative wavy potential $V(q) = -K\cos(2\pi q)$. This research significantly broadens the scope of uniform transportation, shedding light on the diverse and intricate phases of particle dynamics on washboard-like surfaces. In radar systems, the impulse reply holds significant value as it directly influences radar image clarity, object identification accuracy, and associated metrics. This paper focuses on enhancing impulse reply estimation methods, specifically addressing two common challenges: initial gate placement and boundary detection. Traditional approaches either demand substantial prior data or are susceptible to errors in boundary detection shifting along signal variations. To address these issues, we developed the Impulse Reply Estimation via Adaptable Local Projections (IREAL) method. IREAL incorporates both local signal and adaptive gate techniques, allowing for automatic initial gate placement and boundary detection without relying on prior information. Furthermore, we incorporate vector data projections and $\ell_0$-regularized least squares to derive the IREAL solution. Through simulations and real-world data analysis, we demonstrate IREAL's superiority over established techniques. Notably, IREAL outperforms Vector Data Projected Lasso (VDPL) and Single Target Autofocus (STA) in terms of target size accuracy, and surpasses STA in initial gate placement and boundary detection auto-determination. Additionally, the proposed IREAL is shown to outperform other established techniques such as Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC), Multiple Signal Classification with Point Estimate (MUSICPE), and LASSO. To facilitate clear communication, each method is presented in both its mathematical and algorithmic representations, along with corresponding MATLAB execution orders. Finally, the numerical and practical implementation results confidently establish the IREAL as a superior choice. Nonetheless, further numerical and practical investigation is required to confirm IREAL's robustness in diverse scenarios. The proposed method holds potential for automatic and enhanced radar image and object recognition processes. To confirm this, it is essential to conduct a thorough analysis of IREAL's performance in additional practical scenarios. The derived algorithm is currently being considered for auto-radar image and object recognition applications within a company known as NI Ltd., where it has the potential to be integrated into their proprietary software and hardware. Following successful testing, it is likely that IREAL will be published in a renowned journal such as IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing. The detailed analysis and resulting findings will help determine if IREAL is a suitable and robust technology for radar-based systems. The next step in this process is to conduct a thorough numerical and practical investigation. To confirm the proposed method's performance in real-world scenarios, it is essential to collect and analyze data, evaluate the existing techniques, and then compare them with IREAL's proposed implementation. The goal of this analysis is to identify and address the limitations of existing technologies and propose an improved method

We investigate the quantum properties of the electromagnetic field in an environment with a Landau charge, characterised by a finite magnetic flux and zero temperature. The boundary conditions for the electromagnetic radiation are defined by a two-dimensional moving charge experiencing Landau levels. The electromagnetic field is described by angular momentum and entropy associated with a two-dimensional plane and a three-dimensional bulge surrounding the moving charge. The entropy contribution from the plane and the plate's edge are proportional to the magnetic flux, while the bulk entropy satisfies the third law of thermodynamics. The study demonstrates that the angular momentum and entropy associated with a Landau charge exhibit a monotonic dependency on the magnetic flux, much like the behavior of integer quantum Hall states. Additionally, the analysis covers a scenario where the magnetic field confines radiation in a bulge-shaped structure, revealing that the third law applies regardless of the system's size or motion speed. Interestingly, this approach can also describe the conditions under which the magnetic flux can induce non-zero vacuum angular momentum and entropy, even when the temperature reaches absolute zero. The various examples provided emphasize that, despite differing sizes and shapes, the system's properties remain essentially unchanged. Moreover, this concept can be extended to the study of radiation entropy in the context of the jet phenomenon observed in black holes, where the disk's efficient entanglement of radiation with the Black Hole's boundary results in a non-zero bulk entropy contribution that approaches zero at asymptotic infinity. The study also brings forth the idea that the vacuum entropy of a Vainshtein sphere may potentially be a non-zero, finite value, where the radius of the sphere diverges as the temperature approaches absolute zero. However, this scenario is characterized by a specific size condition, where the geometric radius and the quantum radius, described by the Einstein radius of a scattering event, differ significantly, resulting in a non-zero and finite entropy value. The investigation of these concepts lays the groundwork for the understanding that a quantised vacuum in various scenarios, characterized by finite angular momentum and entropy, may potentially be regarded as a conserved quantity, advancing the idea in the direction of Heisenberg's universal constant, where the constant value may imply a unified, non-divergent entropy and angular momentum density. The approach presented brings forth the notion that the vacuum itself may be regarded as a charged particle in a magnetic field, where the third law applies to the environment surrounding the charged particle. Fine-grained named entity recognition in texts involves categorizing entities into their most precise forms by analyzing their meanings, which often requires in-depth semantic analysis. For example, understanding that "United Nations Convention on Refugees" is not related to "United States conventions" demands a level of comprehension beyond normal language models can provide. In our research, we present a novel approach called FGNET-RH that performs this in-depth classification by using a specific geometric structure, known as hyperbolic space. By employing a two-layered approach that integrates the capabilities of a pre-trained model and a small, specialized neural network, our method achieves more accurate outcomes than current techniques. Our research is supported by extensive experiments and evaluations that examine how different elements, including the choice of space and others, impact the overall performance. Our findings indicate that FGNET-RH reaches new peaks in accuracy when compared to other advanced models on various benchmark datasets. The source code for this work can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/fgnet-rh. FGNET-RH has also been hosted on HuggingFace Model Hub at https://huggingface.co/dar-kg/fgnet-rh.

It demonstrates that the Hankel determinants can be expressed as the first Hankel determinant of a new starlike function, involving a parameter from the class $\mathcal{Q}$ introduced in a previous study. Subsequently, it finds the Hankel determinants' lower bounds through the method of majorization. Finally, it presents specific instances to illustrate the findings. Interestingly, it discovers that the Hankel determinants can take on negative values, a first-of-its-kind outcome in the study of Hankel determinants for analytic functions. To verify this, a specific function is constructed that demonstrates this property. Lastly, it explores the relationship between the Hankel determinants and the Hankel transform in harmonic analysis. With the aid of the PDE approach, it demonstrates that the Hankel determinants cannot be expressed as the first Hankel determinant of a function belonging to the class $\mathcal{U}$ or $\mathcal{S}$. Ultimately, it presents a conjecture regarding the Hankel determinants' behavior in the class $\mathcal{U}$ and the general class $\mathcal{S}$. The conjecture suggests that the Hankel determinants can only take positive values, a property that has been observed in previous studies. However, it requires verification for the class $\mathcal{S}$ and the general class $\mathcal{S}^{\ast}$. To support this conjecture, a specific function is constructed that demonstrates positive Hankel determinants. Nonetheless, it is noted that the question whether the Hankel determinants can be expressed as the first Hankel determinant of a function belonging to the class $\mathcal{S}$ or the general class $\mathcal{S}$ remains unresolved. In the future, it aims to investigate and resolve this problem. Additionally, it aims to explore and discover new outcomes for the Hankel determinants in the study of analytic and general classes of conformal mappings. However, since users often reserve resources without utilizing them, we face the challenge of optimizing resource allocation to minimize waste. To address this, we propose Virtual Machine Prepartition, an innovative scheme that simultaneously schedules and partitions reserved resources before virtualization, ensuring effective and efficient allocation. By combining dynamic reservation pricing with offline scheduling and partitioning, we aim to improve system performance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that Virtual Machine Prepartition achieves up to a 32.8% higher throughput and up to a 21.9% lower latency compared to traditional approaches, especially in scenarios with a large number of users. Additionally, we found that the benefit of our approach increases as the number of reserved resources and users grows. Our results highlight the value of prepartitioning in enhancing the performance of cloud data centers. To further improve performance, we have developed Postpartition, a load-distribution strategy that complements Prepartition and enables efficient load distribution among multiple servers. By dynamically dividing load among servers and transferring pending network packets to optimize load distribution, our experiments show that Postpartition significantly enhances Prepartition's performance, improving throughput by up to 11.2% and reducing latency by up to 8.4%. Our results indicate that the combination of Prepartition and Postpartition achieves better results than traditional approaches such as DRS and FlowManager. Furthermore, the performance improves as the number of reserved resources increases. To study complex scenes, it's essential to consider multiple potential interactions and outcomes, which can be achieved by analyzing equilibria for various scenarios.  Expert humans seamlessly predict and evaluate fixed points in numerous contexts, from imagining a person's potential positions to assessing the stability of a political system.  However, capturing these expert judgments poses significant challenges for machines due to the inherently unstable nature of fixed point problems.  Despite advancements in neural networks that employ fixed-point iteration as a solver, there's still a gap in machine understanding of expert-like reasoning about complex scenarios with multiple fixed points.  We present fixed-point networks (FPNs), which leverage the dynamics-based representation of neural networks to successfully track and predict fixed points without getting stuck in local optima.  Through training FPNs on spatial prediction tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of stabilizing the loss function using a large coefficient to replicate expert-like reasoning and achieve state-of-the-art performance in robotic planning and social understanding benchmarks.  Importantly, FPNs provide a natural foundation for incorporating prior knowledge and expert examples, enabling the transfer of knowledge across domains and allowing modifications to be propagated through optimization.  Ultimately, FPNs open up new avenues for integrating expert insights, transferring knowledge, and enhancing human-like reasoning in machines.

This study explores ways to measure information sharing between two events using more than 30 distinct metrics. These measures are evaluated in the context of two events, A and B, where A is considered the cause and B the effect. Specifically, the analysis focuses on the physical phenomenon of entanglement, but the concepts are broader and can be applied to other fields as well. To facilitate comparison, the preferences of these measures are determined for events described by single numbers, such as qubits, and events described by larger matrices. This comparison enables a deeper understanding of the limitations of these information measures, particularly when one event has a limited number of possible outcomes, and when the correlation between A and B is substantial. Furthermore, the analysis highlights potential difficulties in accurately assessing information sharing in complex scenarios with many dimensions. To illustrate this challenge, the analysis shows that varying information measures yield vastly different results for events that differ by only small amounts, thus underscoring their limited reliability. This issue is characterized as the loss of transitivity, where the relationship between causes and effects becomes inconsequential due to the large number of dimensions involved, thus emphasizing the importance of carefully considering information measures based on their underlying principles. Finally, the analysis shows that certain information measures can serve as strict criteria for determining whether one event causes another. Specifically, the analysis reveals that perfect correlation between A and B is a necessary condition for A causing B, and that requiring B to have multiple possible outcomes is a necessary condition for A causing B. This paper extends the concept of S-rings, initially defined within the context of locally Noetherian rings by Avriopoulos and Katsaros, to arbitrary rings. It's demonstrated that any such ring possesses a unique largest Noetherian subring, comprising the intersection of all Noetherian subrings, which is itself Noetherian. This subring can be characterized as the subring consisting of zero divisors or more broadly, consisting of elements admitting left or two-sided annihilators within the original ring. These subrings are identified as the largest such subrings when the original ring is either topos or left Noetherian. Moreover, it's proven that they possess properties analogous to those of locally Noetherian S-rings. Specifically, any ideal within these subrings is automatically contained within the largest such subring of left Noetherian or two-sided annihilators, while preserving the ascending chain condition (ACC) within that subring. This result complements and enhances the findings of Avriopoulos and Katsaros, applied in the context of locally Noetherian rings. Additionally, as part of the methodology employed in this investigation, it's shown that any ring possessing only transversal chains, or satisfying the conditions for weakly Noetherian or quasi-Noetherian in either the left or two-sided context, can be characterized equivalently as having an S-ring of two-sided annihilators. This, in turn, allows for the determination of conditions under which these types of rings can be further characterized as either left or two-sided Noetherian. These conditions include, for instance, the requirement that any left ideal within the ring is such that any chain of extensions is itself a chain within the ring. Similarly, it's proven that any quasi-Noetherian ring of two-sided annihilators must satisfy the condition that any chain of extensions is itself a chain within the ring. All these findings are then translated and expressed within the context of prime rings. As a consequence of this, it's ultimately shown that any prime ring containing an S-ring of two-sided annihilators itself possesses an S-ring of two-sided annihilators, while an analogous result is identified for locally Noetherian rings, where it's found that any ring containing an S-ring of two-sided annihilators is itself contained within an locally Noetherian S-ring of two-sided annihilators. To accommodate rapidly multiplying IoT gadgets and minimizing latency in monitoring, cutting-edge surveillance systems are required. They must incorporate low-latency monitoring while guaranteeing maximum surveillance efficiency. In monitoring systems, the interconnection of multiple monitoring modules is crucial for achieving optimal effectiveness. However, in existing surveillance systems, each module is separate, and modules may sometimes miss despite repeated attempts to connect. In this study, a locational monitoring approach is introduced for IoT devices using a private blockchain to tackle these issues. A novel gadget relationship model is developed to enhance surveillance effectiveness, rigorously defining the relationship between multiple gadgets including their spatial localization. By utilizing a private blockchain to validate transactions in the gadget network, the robustness of the surveillance system is ensured. In order to enhance surveillance performance, a customized routing algorithm is designed to adaptively choose the shortest path for data transmission. Achieved results indicate that the locational monitoring approach significantly boosts surveillance effectiveness by efficiently reducing the number of missed notifications. Additionally, the convergence time of the surveillance system is greatly minimized. Achieved results embody the significance of this research, showcasing its potential to streamline monitoring processes. Performance assessments demonstrate that the proposed surveillance system outperforms current solutions in terms of surveillance effectiveness and latency. For example, the optimization of the routing table enhances the effectiveness of surveillance by 25.86%, while simultaneous monitoring by multiple modules decreases latency by 51.08%. Results of performance evaluations further validate these claims. Moreover, future research scopes are outlined at the conclusion. Firstly, the proposed framework could be applied to incorporate more sophisticated strategies for choosing the most suitable module for intermodule communication despite module selection policies employed in existing surveillance systems. Secondly, additional locational information such as the distance and angle between gadgets can be utilized to further enhance surveillance effectiveness and latency. Thirdly, additional features of the IoT devices under surveillance such as processing power, quality of service, quality of service rate, and quality of service delay, could be leveraged to further maximize surveillance effectiveness and minimize latency. In summary, additional features of the IoT devices under surveillance could be leveraged to further maximize surveillance effectiveness and minimize latency. A comprehensive dataset consisting of various parameters including signal strength, latitude, and longitude is also provided for replication purposes. In addition to the dataset, open-source code for replicating the surveillance system is also made available. Additionally, a video illustrating the surveillance system is also included. In conclusion, this research makes a significant contribution to surveillance systems through its innovative dataset construction and code sharing, thereby paving the way for generalizing its outcomes to other domains.

A widely employed modulation technique, gray coding, is utilized in numerous communication systems and computing hardware due to its straightforward conversion to binary encoding and its ability to promote error detection in convolutional codes. Although easy to implement, its decoding approach can be complicated. In current digital coding methods, determining the logical values, L-values, and constructing binary codes using these values are often separate processes with each responsible for half of the decoding difficulties. Integrating these processes may therefore reduce decoding challenges. However, traditional approaches that combine L-values and binary codes through look-up tables encounter pretraining biases during the training of neural networks for binary coding. In our research, we propose a novel approach called "L-value quantization" that determines multiple L-values simultaneously and demonstrates the potential of combining L-values and binary codes through a single end-to-end training process. Our approach can eliminate pretraining biases and achieves accurate results in both synthetic and real-world scenarios with reduced decoding difficulties. Additionally, it significantly decreases the size of gray codes in both theoretical and experimental analyses. Our results also compare favorably with existing approaches in both theoretical and experimental analyses. Our approach can be applied to a broad spectrum of communication systems and computing hardware that rely on gray coding. In our study, we applied our approach to a Gray-coded adaptive filter and observed an approximately 26 percent reduction in the size of the non-quantized binary codes without compromising filter performance, exceeding the theoretical limit of a previously published approach by 2.5 percent. Our approach can potentially accelerate wireless communication, lower energy consumption in computing hardware, and stimulate further research in machine learning-based coding techniques. Our study of L-value quantization through deep learning has also inspired research in other areas of coding theory. Our results suggest that some coding difficulties may stem from inadequate training data. In our study, we employed two neural networks, applied them to input data, and selected the output from one as the final output, demonstrating the potential for using multiple codewords to increase decoding accuracy and reduce decoding difficulties. Our study also employed vectorization to accelerate the decoding process, but other approaches, such as compression and quantization, may further increase execution speed. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of coding problems. In our study, we employed two neural networks because the selected output may depend on the performance of both networks, but other coding techniques may utilize just one network. Our results have also inspired research in using the Fisher Jensen Shannon kernel to determine whether codewords can be utilized to increase decoding accuracy and reduce decoding difficulties. Covering arrays (CA) and strength-2 covering arrays in particular have received considerable research attention. While there have been extensive investigations into the general properties of CA, most previous studies focused specifically on the parameters of CA related to two parameters: index α and size σ. However, this paper seeks to explore a distinct subset of CA characterized by low values for both α and σ, specifically those with index less than or equal to 2 and size less than or equal to 3. We refer to this subset as the minor strength-2 CA family. Through the introduction of additional parameters, a generalized framework is established to study minor strength-2 CA. We identify, construct and compare different types of minor strength-2 CA, including special cases such as rectangular arrays, relative covering arrays and weakly 2-covering biarrays. A comprehensive review is conducted on over 1700 minor strength-2 CA instances, covering a combined range of 19,900,960 possible parameter values. Our study provides a foundation for future research on minor strength-2 CA, offering an extensive set of examples to test the efficiency of algorithms designed to generate or cover these arrays. Ultimately, this research is aimed at fostering an in-depth investigation into the attributes of minor strength-2 CA and other minor strength-k CA. We also visualize some prospective questions that can be answered through a study of minor strength-2 CA, such as finding or constructing CA with various additional properties, and analyzing the relationship between the parameters of CA, in particular, the parameters related to weakly d-covering arrays. A mathematical description and key properties of minor strength-k covering arrays is provided in the appendix. We also provide a guide on how to use these arrays effectively in combinatorial algorithms in the appendix. Moreover, our study offers a chance to explore the quasi-polynomial complexity of algorithms to generate or cover special types of minor strength-2 CA, such as semi-orthogonal, semi-orthogonal with row strength-2, and green-red arrays. The examination also opens up the possibility of further investigation into the potential for detecting and measuring the complex properties of the quark-gluon plasma through thermal photons and other probe particles. It is hypothesized that future experiments may be able to exploit these properties to gain a deeper understanding of the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. This rare occurrence was likely triggered by a shock wave produced by an expanding jet of plasma that pushed against the coronal surface. Although the source of the jet is still unknown, experts believe it could be associated with the onset of a sunspot phase or a complex system of magnetic loops. Researchers have also found that the coronal surface is surprisingly more rigid than expected, requiring extremely high pressures to undergo significant changes. This discovery implies that the coronal surface is characterized by a high degree of "micro-resistance." Additionally, the measurement of the shock wave's speed and the surrounding plasma conditions has provided the first first-principles estimate of the coronal surface's temperature, yielding a value consistent with established temperature gradients. This incident serves as an exemplary case for testing the principles of MHD simulations of the solar atmosphere and demonstrates how the production of radio waves can facilitate our comprehension of these complex systems. Furthermore, the measurement of the dark light's frequency and the push of the expanding jet against the coronal surface allows scientists to determine the temperature of the coronal surface, yielding a value that is consistent with established temperature gradients. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), including variants such as LSTMs and GRUs, pose significant challenges in distributed deep learning scenarios, particularly in contexts involving communication efficiency and data privacy. Existing approaches that employ recursive techniques like DP-REC are optimized for communication efficiency but compromise data privacy due to potential gradient explosions. In response, we present a new approach, DP-GREC, an efficient and private variant of the GReEN algorithm designed for communication efficiency and data privacy. DP-GREC achieves this through the application of the dual gradient method and the application of both differential privacy and quantization techniques. We theorize that recursive algorithms may suffer from significant gradient growth, and we validate this by demonstrating significant gradient growth in popular deep learning algorithms, including RNN variants, under certain conditions. Based on this, we leverage techniques like DP-GREED, which combines gradient clipping, to mitigate gradient growth. Our experimental results show that DP-GREC is superior to other approaches, including Scippa, DP-REC, and Federated Learning with local updates, delivering a 36.7% reduced communication overhead while providing superior test accuracy and improved privacy guarantees. And furthermore, we show that DP-GREC outperforms DP-REC, providing 1.5x improved test accuracy with reduced communication overhead. Finally, we show that under strict communication limitations, DP-GREC is the only viable solution, highlighting its value in real-world distributed learning settings where communication efficiency and data privacy are critical. Long-term demographic changes are being driven by significant migration trends 
and rapid fertility declines, resulting in extensive dispersal patterns of people 
from urban centers. To effectively conduct population surveys, particularly in remote 
areas, researchers must consider the evolving population landscape. To address this, 
a survey-based approach called survey autonomous population estimation is employed, 
which is particularly useful for understanding sparse populations in emerging cities. 
We developed a comprehensive framework combining population estimation algorithms 
with a survey management system, optimized with a heuristic called the within-window 
score. We successfully tested this system in two recent surveys of the Maputo's 
periphery in Mozambique, yielding accurate population size predictions and a 
systematic assessment of population coverage. Our results indicate that the 
implementation of this system has reduced the number of survey participants needed to 
achieve the desired level of coverage by 30% and enhance the quality of population 
coverage by 10-15%. We are confident that this system will continue to show 
improvements as it is applied in additional surveys. Additionally, we propose 
additional surveys to assess the method's effectiveness and efficiency. 
This research has several potential applications and could be adapted for other areas 
where population surveys are a priority, especially in cities experiencing similar 
trends of external migration and declining fertility rates. 
Furthermore, we maintain a public repository of the system's code, along with 
the data collected from our recent surveys in Maputo. 
This work was approved by the University of Mozambique's ethics committee with 
the reference number CE/FIL/012/2021. 
To guarantee the confidentiality of the population, our approach eliminates any 
personal identity-related information in the estimated population dataset.

from the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research.

This study introduces a novel method using filters to collect data with the guarantee of containing no false positives, relying on estimating query memberships for an optimal approach. The proposed strategy composes a method that can, given a dataset $D$, produce a subset $\hat{M}$ of $D$, and a parameter $\epsilon$ between 0 and 1, such that the probability of $\hat{M}$ containing all true members of $D$ is at least $1-\epsilon$. The collection strategy proposed here has a predictable relationship with $\epsilon$ and the size of $\hat{M}$, with an upper limit of $\epsilon^{1/\alpha}$ for a specific $\alpha$ value, and this bound can be reached in some cases. The size of $\hat{M}$ is decided by an $\alpha$ value which can be influenced for better $\epsilon$ values. The authors also present a method to pick the most suitable $\alpha$ given an $\epsilon$ value, and this allows the creation of an algorithm that can gather a dataset $\hat{D}$ from a given dataset $D$, such that $\hat{D}$ contains no false positives with high probability, and the size of $\hat{D}$ is close to the size of a nearly-exact dataset $\tilde{D}$ obtained through an approximate membership query method. The authors also present two applications, one for finding a subset of labels in a multi-label dataset, and another for gathering data for supervised learning in a classification task. The proposed strategy has a predictable relationship between the size of the collected data and the likelihood of false results in a classification task. This integrated framework utilizes a multi-phase kinematic model coupled with a fluid-structure interaction algorithm and is particularly suited for scenarios involving light-to-heavy fluid interactions. Numerous experimental and theoretical test cases are employed to validate the framework's accuracy, efficiency, and stability before demonstrating its practical application in analyzing the dynamics of a cavitating hydraulic turbine model. Compared to conventional SPH methods, the proposed framework yields significant improvements in cavity size reduction, drag minimization, and computational efficiency, along with an overall revival rate of approximately 90%. With advancements in telecommunications, controlling devices remotely has become a reality. This concept is known as telepresence, enabling users to seamlessly interact with a device from a distant location. This study focuses on assessing the quality of service experience in a specific telepresence scenario - controlling robots with a first-person view - and asks participants to evaluate their experience interacting with a remote robot as if they were actually sitting in the driver's seat. The research compares the QoE of users under various delay conditions, using a method that simulates real-world delays and an online survey to gather users' perceived levels of frustration. The experimental findings are then analyzed using a statistical model to identify how delay affects QoE in this context and how this experience varies based on the level of interaction, whether the user is navigating or controlling the robot, and whether the user is using the device for entertainment or education purposes. The study further examines how a particular delay phenomenon, known as packet delay variation, influences QoE in this context. The research provides quantitative values for how delay impacts QoE in this scenario, offering an effective method to evaluate and improve the quality of service and user experience in similar applications. This study was presented at the conference ICQN 2021, where it received the Best Paper Award, and the results have been validated through a follow-up user study. The results demonstrate that very short delays can still impact QoE negatively, that interacting with a robot is more demanding than simply watching a video, and that demonstrating a strategy to manage these delays can improve the user's overall experience. Finally, the research highlights the importance of considering the specific application when evaluating the impact of delay on QoE and using a method to synthesize a range of realistic, variable delays can generate more accurate and useful QoE models. Such an approach could lead to a significant improvement in the quality of service and user experience in a range of telecommunications applications, including telepresence systems. In numerous scientific fields and high-dimensional data analysis, clustering has gained significant interest due to its numerous applications. The primary objective of clustering is to group data points based on similarity. The weighted fuzzy k-means algorithm has been utilized for this purpose, but its effectiveness depends on the pre-defined weights, which can be challenging to determine in high-dimensional datasets. The entropy of a data set can be used to evaluate its irregularity and inform the weights used in clustering, as well as provide clustering validity measures. The ability of the fuzzy k-means method to handle noise and interpret cluster characteristics makes it a good choice for processing data of unknown shape and dimension. The proposed FKWkMea approach integrates k-means clustering and fuzzy c-means algorithms to determine optimal weights for clustering, and evaluates its performance using 40 real datasets and four metrics, comparing results with state-of-the-art methods. The datasets utilized were drawn from diverse domains, and the effectiveness of the FKWkMea approach was assessed using evaluation metrics such as within-cluster cohesion, within-cluster spacing, silhouette coefficient and Chernoff bounding sphere overlap. The performance of the FKWkMea method surpassed existing clustering algorithms in terms of several clustering metrics in the evaluation using real datasets. The approach achieved an average performance of 0.6126 in the silhouette coefficient and 0.0397 in the Chernoff bounding sphere overlap metrics, outperforming other methods. The proposed FKWkMea approach was found to be computationally efficient, processing a dataset of 50000 samples in approximately 45 seconds. The results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of the FKWkMea method in clustering datasets of diverse dimensions with reduced computational complexity. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial in various applications and are part of many powerful neural networks. However, training such models frequently gets stuck in local Optimal Policy solutions where an Expert takes on all tasks, leading to poor performance. Current methods fail to overcome this problem, even with prolonged training and extended observation periods. We introduce a novel class of algorithms, dubbed Indirect Algorithms, which induce a unique dynamics where all experts can consistently improve parameters in sync with the current Optimistic Basic Policy, thereby breaking the deadlock and achieving superior results on demanding MoE tasks. Indirect Algorithms consistently guarantee convergence and train Indirect Basic Policy to the optimal solution efficiently in just two updates, outperforming state-of-the-art methods, including those reported in "Efficient and Reliable Algorithms for Mixture-of-Experts" [2021]. We also leverage our method to improve performance in challenging tasks, such as reliable uncertainty estimation, reinforcement learning with rare events, reinforcement learning in dynamic environments, and more. Ultimately, our approach enables the creation of highly efficient neural networks with accurate gage and generative functions. We demonstrate this potential by developing a neural network with accurate classification and p-value prediction on CIFAR-10 with just 6 trainable parameters. Such a small network enables our method to identify meaningful patterns in ShapeNet, leading to state-of-the-art reinforcement learning in 3D environments despite only using 20 Experts. Furthermore, our approach allows us to design a large-scale reinforcement learning agent with efficient and reliable capacity on Grid World Large Image data. A specific, combinatorial formula for the branch number is given when the graph has a particular structure called a flower graph, consisting of a central vertex connected to three distinct leaves. This study examines the influence of quantum gravity on tensor fluctuations within the primordial universe, ultimately constraining the impact on primordial cosmic birefringence. Although tensor fluctuations are suppressed in many quantum gravity theories featuring global symmetry disruption, we deviate from prior studies by incorporating an important symmetry breaking phase transition. By accurately determining the irrelevant dimensions of kinetic terms for three-dimensional global symmetry tensors, we validated a previous estimate and derived a more precise relation. Furthermore, through a meromorphic partition function and a new estimate for the irreducible quantum gravity dimension, the ratio of gauge to platonian amplitudes was explicitly calculated in four-dimensional space-time, leading to a constraint on quantum gravity theories with global symmetry disruption and their associated effects on cosmic birefringence. Our analysis indicates that cosmic birefringine observations can refine lower bounds on the irreducible dimension of tensor operators by at least four orders of magnitude and similarly refine the ratio of gauge to platonian amplitudes, thereby constraining quantum gravity theories. To ensure its accuracy and safety, thorough testing of its performance is vital, particularly in cases where its training data may have been representative of a specific population, but its application is expanded to encompass others. To address this challenge, a novel method called Conformal Forecasting is proposed to assess AI-powered medical devices under real-world distribution shifts. This approach involves creating a predictive model, referred to as the main model, and utilizing an auxiliary model, often referred to as the reference model, to estimate the main model's uncertainty in predicting specific individuals. By analyzing the differences in predicted and actual performance across multiple individuals, a measure of the model's uncertainty or error is calculated. To illustrate the efficacy of this methodology in practical terms, an experimental study was conducted utilizing the UltraVista scanner, demonstrating how an auxiliary model, trained solely through induced perturbations, can be used to identify potential misdiagnosis and suggest alternative interpretations. This potential application represents an area for further investigation. Through our study, we gained practical insight into the effectiveness of the proposed methodology in assessing AI-powered medical devices under real-world distribution shifts. Furthermore, we obtained key statistical insights into the parameters influencing the performance of the auxiliary model, including a marked preference for models with lower epistemic uncertainty over those with higher. In a specific type of molecular dynamics simulation called Atomic Masking, the charges on certain simulated atoms can be modified to replicate the effects of specific experimental techniques. The setup of these charges is critical to the success of the simulation, with an emphasis typically placed on the DNA's phosphate groups. However, this study explores an alternative approach, fixing the diatomic charges but allowing the hydrogen atoms to move freely and introduce negative bias on the oxygen atoms, resulting in a significant electrostatic shift towards the end with the oxygen charge. As a result, DNA models with greater tension between the two strands were obtained, along with increased backbone flexibility and a reduced average helical twist. Additionally, the findings of this simulation suggest that stiffening the base bias, as opposed to simply increasing the helical twist, is required to replicate the effects of base pair propensities in discrete molecular dynamics simulations of DNA. Furthermore, the utility of this approach is demonstrated through the identification of specific target recognition motifs that differ from those obtained in standard simulations. The implications of these results are discussed in the context of understanding the mechanisms behind specific molecular processes. ANS arithmetic incorporates two novel components: simplified addition and subtraction and a method for multiplying any two integers, which has the added benefit of producing a partial or full carry if the products exceed the bit length. Our analysis demonstrates that modulo 10 multiplicative operations can lead to a compression rate of up to 90%, while also outlining the requirements for achieving the highest compression rate. The dielectric properties of materials are influenced by the dielectric properties of their constituent fluids. In cement-based materials, pore fluid plays a crucial role in determining the dielectric properties of the material as a whole. Therefore, understanding how the dielectric properties of pore fluid evolve over time is essential in creating accurate models that predict material behavior using dielectric testing. This study examines the dielectric properties of three different pore fluids (water, sodium lactate solution, and 1M sodium solution) at various concentrations and temperatures, and explores the impact of cement paste and capillary effects on measured results. Moreover, it discusses the applicability of dielectric testing on cement-based materials contaminated by pore fluids. To this end, dielectric properties were measured using impedance spectroscopy across a broad frequency range, and the results were translated into equivalent AC conductivity measurements. Results are presented in the form of dielectric permittivity, dielectric conductivity, and dielectric properties graphs, which demonstrate the distinct dielectric behavior of each fluid. Dielectric properties were found to be temperature-independent but dependent on concentration, resulting in higher dielectric properties in the presence of cement paste and capillary effects. Frequency-dependent dielectric behavior was observed through the calculation of dielectric permittivity and conductivity. Ultimately, results indicate that dielectric testing can be an effective means for monitoring cement-based materials contaminated by pore fluids if proper fluid selection, concentration, and porosity are taken into account. Based on these findings, two criteria for dielectric testing were proposed and applied to validate the results. One of the criteria, based on dielectric permittivity, suggests that dielectric properties lie below the upper bound defined by pure fluid results, while the second criterion, based on dielectric conductivity, indicates that dielectric properties lie within the frequency-dependent range of the pure fluid conductivity. Dielectric tests were performed to compare the three different pore fluids (water, sodium lactate solution, and 1M sodium solution) to assess their potential for cement-based materials contaminated detection and monitoring. As a result, sodium lactate solution emerged as the preferred pore fluid, exhibiting distinct dielectric behavior that could be used to contamant detection and monitoring, whereas the other two pore fluids exhibited less distinct dielectric behavior. Ultimately, sodium lactate solution may be used as a reference or control fluid in dielectric testing, given its inherent characteristics can be replicated in the formulation of model-based coatings to enhance coating adhesion to cement-based materials. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest at high redshifts is a prime observational tool for understanding the interplay between galaxies and the intergalactic medium through the absorption spectra of distant quasars. Analysis of its complexities has been hindered by a lack of sufficient data and inadequate frameworks for interpreting patterns within the data. To mitigate these limitations, researchers have developed new methods to extract cosmological information, including a novel approach that utilizes three-dimensional correlations while minimizing the impact of low-resolution spectra. Demonstrated on simulated data, these techniques yield precise results even in the presence of poor data, paving the way for applications with current and future observations to derive precise measurements of the parameters governing structure and evolution across cosmic time. Furthermore, these pipelines can be adapted to enable statistical searches for non-standard physics and the study of complex ion distribution phases. Observational applications will refine the parameters and reveal subtle variations in cosmic structure, while showcasing the potential to unlock the full potential of upcoming observations. The complete code for these applications is available for download. 

Our pipelines generate three-dimensional correlation functions by averaging along narrow channels and visualize how they change with scale variations, redshift, and ion distribution phases. To correct for distortions caused by large-scale structure, we use perturbation theory, while modeling the s-scale by assuming a log-normal distribution of absorptions. This model is then normalized using a constrained Gaussian process incorporating mock correlations and a prior for the mean transmission. 

Our analysis of synthetic data at z=2, 4, and 5 finds that without priors on the mean transmission, three-dimensional correlations can constrain the parameter sigma_8, while incorporating priors enables constraints on other parameters, including nonlinear matter, reionization timing, and neutrino properties. To demonstrate this, we consider two scenarios: one in which three-dimensional correlations are complete, and another in which they are partially sampled. 

Our results show that three-dimensional correlations can constrain cosmological parameters such as sigma_8, n_s, and H_0 by nearly an order of magnitude, while also placing limits on the baryon acoustic oscillation feature and neutrino properties. 

However, when considering parameter degeneracies, we find that three-dimensional correlations can pin down the time of reionization, while models including cold dark matter are required to fully explore the parameter space available in future observations.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully observed, for the first time, the transfer of transverse and longitudinal beam emittances between two adjacent cavities in a linear accelerator, specifically using the Advanced Proton Source's radio frequency quadrupole cavity and its adjacent linac cavity.  This breakthrough has significant implications for future linear accelerators, particularly regarding coupling and impedance issues that may impede low-energy beam propagation, a concern that could potentially compromise efforts to establish a high-intensity, beam-based neutron source.  To study emittance coupling, scientists used the APS Linac on an unprecedented scale, spanning from DC to 2 GHz, with their findings (published in the Physical Review Special Topics) revealing a notable level of emittance coupling and a method for determining coupling and an introduction to techniques for evaluating impedance in accelerator systems.  This experiment marked a new approach in experimental methodology, one that could be applied to other research areas, while its conclusions provide essential background for evaluating and optimizing beam transport systems and a case for further research in superconducting accelerator technology. In various fields, measures of complexity have proven effective in identifying stages of development, yet they lack consistency when applied across different systems. This study investigates and contrasts information-theoretic metrics of complexity in Boltzmann machines, demonstrating that a measure may not adequately capture a system's progression to higher levels of organization. Conversely, alternative measures may offer a more accurate representation, and the data suggests that mutual information could serve as a potential metric. Furthermore, it is observed that a system in equilibrium tends to exhibit minimal or no complexity, and the rate at which a system becomes more disordered may be slower than the rate at which it becomes less disorderly. This phenomenon is characterized as an asymmetric rate of order/disorder transition. The implications of these findings are discussed in the context of information-theoretic metrics of complexity. It is suggested that a diverse range of metrics should be utilized in quantitative analyses of complexity to minimize the risk of incorrect conclusions. Nonetheless, the data presented offers initial support for the potential of mutual information as a measure of complexity. Additionally, the concept of asymmetric order/disorder transitions offers valuable insights for the design of systems capable of adapting and learning through Boltzmann machines. This design principle is expected to prove relevant in the study of information-theoretic measures and artificial neural networks. Finally, various potential applications and extensions of the study's findings are explored. They are expected to be valid in the study of natural neural networks, as well as other systems exhibiting temporal and spatial organization. Moreover, the study offers a theoretical foundation for the design of artificial systems capable of adapting and learning, with a focus on the study of thermodynamic systems and artificial adaptive systems. Importantly, the study offers a synthesis of the work in the fields of art, philosophy, and science, with a focus on the study of temporal and spatial organization. While the study is largely theoretical, it is expected that the concepts and data analyzed can inform the design of the study system. Recent advancements in the control of quantum states have led to proposals for adjusting quantum systems in such a way that the final state is not randomly assembled but instead is constructed through a smooth, gradual change from an initial stable state, preserving its properties until the end of the process. This approach has been explored in the context of adiabatic perturbations and within the context of quantum learning. However, there is still no comprehensive theory available that can be applied flexibly to drive quantum systems in this way. This article presents a new method for modifying Hamiltonians to produce desired outcomes while preserving initial stability, specifically employing a variational approach. This method was demonstrated with the Hubbard model, allowing the assembly of crystalline ground states through a variational strategy that is resilient to counterdiabatic perturbations and can be easily simulated using traditional dynamics equations. Notably, our results indicate that incorporating realistic spin-orbit coupling and considerable interactions in the Hubbard model does not complicate the process of assembling the ground state. This method has the potential to be applied to more complex quantum systems, enabling the creation of new pathways for state transition that are driven by a variational approach. It could also serve as a foundation for quantum algorithms powered by learning, potentially leading to the development of novel applications in the realm of simulated quantum matter. Furthermore, our results could also contribute to the study of quantum dynamics through the investigation of adjustable Hamiltonian driving transformations. Research into the properties of crystals using the Hubbard model, coupled with proposals for implementing the method using quantum light and precise nuclear motion, illustrate the potential of this approach in the simulation of quantum matter with quantum systems. Several potential applications and extensions are discussed, including connections to related works that construct driving transformations via quantum composable operations, quantum learning, and simultaneous steering of multiple quantum systems. Image color information can be represented in various distinct domains, including the RGB and CMY color spaces, which offer an alternative to the more traditional XYZ and CIE Lab formats by providing spacial properties in the color domain.  In image processing, the RGB domain is particularly useful for operations such as brightness adjustment, as well as the CMY domain for tasks like multi-exposure fusion and color grading.  Although the CMY color space can be derived from the CIE Lab color representation through an arbitrary 3x3 transformation, a widely used empirical formula for this purpose has been reported to have drawbacks in terms of color preservation and correlated color distortion.  A novel approach, therefore, aims to derive the CMY color representation from the CIE Lab color space via an optimized 3x3 transformation, yielding improved results in terms of yellow and blue axis correlation when compared to the empirical formula.  This new CMY color representation is then applied in the context of high dynamic range (HDR) image tone mapping, with the addition of an innovative color grading technique that utilizes the CMY color space to combine differently exposed images and produce a single HDR image.  Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed color model exhibits better color consistency and accurate hue temperature properties, with the novel HDR image processing technique also shown to outperform existing approaches in terms of combined effectiveness.  Specifically, the proposed method is reported to achieve lower chromaticity distance errors when compared to competing techniques that employ the CMY color space.  This method is particularly effective at preserving color hue, with associated error metrics that significantly underscoring this capability.  A direct comparison with the empirical formula for CMY color representation, reported to result in 11.86% higher error rates in terms of the L2 distance metric, further highlights the benefits of the proposed technique.  This difference in error rates is equally evident in the context of the L-infinite (or max) distance metric, with the proposed method exhibiting improved results.  Quantitative analysis of the methods also includes a comparison of the degree to which the RGB to CMY color transition affects the green color axis, with the proposed method exhibiting lower impact in this case.  This method is further distinguished by its lower 90-90% tolerance region compared to the empirical formula.  This proposed method is consequently deemed a suitable alternative to the empirical formula for deriving the CMY color representation from the CIE Lab color space.  Moreover, when applied in the context of HDR image processing, the proposed method is shown to significantly improve image quality

The limit property of a function f(x) is its behavior as x approaches a specific point, such as c. When f(c) is not equal to zero, this behavior is often described by the function's Taylor series expansion at point c, especially if it can be expressed as an exponential of a power series. Given two functions f(x) and g(x) both equal to the limit of e^(-1/x) as x approaches infinity, this paper examines the higher-order terms of their difference. Interestingly, our research reveals that their difference has exponential behavior in terms of 1/x and its expansion may vary based on the function's original expression. However, when the difference is calculated using e(-1/x)^2] it inevitably yields the same exponential behavior, regardless of the initial function used. Furthermore, our analysis suggests the possibility of applying these findings to other limit properties, such as the behavior of a function as x approaches infinity. As a result, this paper provides comprehensive expansions for three specific limit properties, such as f(x) as x approaches infinity, f(b + 1/x) as x approaches infinity, and f(c) as x approaches c. These expansions can be considered a robust version of the previously known limit properties and may be particularly useful for accelerating the convergence of related expressions. One potential application of these expansions is the reduction of the computational error in numerical methods, such as the weakly nonlocal quadratic convergent power series expansion of the error function. We introduce RDF as a structured text format that preserves relationships, allowing for machine interpretation. To facilitate a seamless transition from relational data, we examine various transfer methods, taking into account diverse source and target data storage systems, as well as RDF libraries. Our focus lies on shaping relational data according to established data models like FOAF and Shape Expressions, which ensure organized and hierarchical storage of RDF data for enhanced query efficiency. By leveraging these shapes, we outline a two-step transfer process, combining relational data into RDF and then organizing the resulting graph according to the defined shape. Our method is demonstrated through a practical application, using real-world relational data to create an RDF graph that effectively maps to various target storage systems, such as RDF databases, key-value stores, and hypertext applications, based on predetermined query requirements. Finally, we validate the efficiency of our approach by comparing it with established RDF building and loading techniques on actual datasets. The research showcases a practical methodology for managing large datasets, from relational databases to RDF graphs, that incorporate shape definitions. We showcase the method's efficacy on a real-world application and highlight its potential for query acceleration. Additionally, we specify two open standards, one for relational data modeling and another for RDF loading, which can enhance existing tools and libraries, including MySQL, RDFDB, and Fuseki, resulting in their extended versions, described in corresponding technical reports. We're investigating how pre-trained language models can be utilized for 
analyzing and understanding natural language without human supervision or 
requiring extensive labeled data. We're concentrating our research into two 
key areas: Firstly, discovering structured data within text using various 
techniques, and how these structures can be found using both automatic and 
human oversight. Secondly, we're exploring methods to accomplish various 
natural language processing tasks using minimal labeled data. We're examining 
two approaches: one relying on pre-trained models that incorporate additional 
explanation mechanisms, and another leveraging transfer learning strategies. 
This methods allow our models to learn from a broader range of tasks than 
previously possible, even when there is an abundance of data within a 
specific task is scarce. We're testing these methods on various tasks such as 
extracting specific entities, identifying the sentiment towards a particular 
text, and summarizing the key points within a document. We're comparing our 
techniques against other state-of-the-art methods and finding that they are 
either equivalent or superior to these methods when there is an abundance of 
unlabeled data available. However, when there is a shortage of labeled data, 
our methods are often outperformed by other approaches such as cross-domain 
transfer. We're investigating additional strategies to tackle this challenge. 
This study ultimately aims to establish a foundation for the development of 
language analysis methods that require little to no human supervision. Such 
methods could, for instance, broaden the scope of natural language datasets, 
enabling analysis through diverse corpora and facilitate more efficient 
training without relying on extensive annotated data sets. This research is 
currently in its early stages, and significant hurdles need to be overcome 
before such methods can be applied effectively in real-world environments.

The accuracy of Speech-to-Text systems has improved significantly over the years,
thanks to the extensive datasets used in model training. While large-scale datasets
exist for English, there is a shortage of such resources for other languages.
To address this, our project involves creating a Kaldi-based model for Open Source
Speech Recognition in German. Our approach includes collecting and compiling
German Audio Corpora and utilizing them to build a highly accurate ASR model.
Using the recently developed xvector-ensemble model, we achieved an impressive
49.2% error rate on the RedDaudio dataset, surpassing the performance of Google
Speech Recognition with a 24.8% margin. By leveraging our Corpora and Kaldi-based
model, we believe that ASR technology for German can be greatly enhanced. The

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however with distinct differences in their predicted characteristics. Through the analysis of spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope of a group of 8 Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus cluster, our research has found them to be rapidly rotating rigid bodies with average rotation speeds of around 300 km per second, which supports the theory of dual evolution pathways. Additionally, our research has found these stars to have lower surface temperatures of around 25000K rather than 30000K and a broader range of temperatures among their sample of Be-type stars in 30 Doradus, in contrast to their classifications. Our research has also found them to have similar properties such as the strength of their helium absorption and the width of their emission lines. Strong evidence was found for helium in the stars' spectra which could not be explained by the stars' rotation alone, however it could be explained by the presence of a solid surface on a rotating ball. Our research has also found evidence of a strong, steady wind, however it was not enough to explain the stars' lack of helium in their atmospheres, which needs to be further investigated. Our research has also found that the stars' synchronised and asynchroneous rotation could explain the difference in the width of their emission lines. Our research suggests that in order to understand Be-type stars it is crucial to consider more than one rotation state and that they should be observed with instruments with the capability of looking deeper into the stars' atmospheres than observational data has previously suggested. Observational data of 8 Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus cluster was analysed through the context of both single and dual evolution theories. Our research has also found evidence for a steady wind in the stars' atmospheres which could not be explained by the stars' rotation rates or surface temperatures of the stars in the cluster of 30 Doradus. Inverse Text Standardization involves transforming varied text formats into a uniform format for text information extraction in datasets. This process is necessary for text datasets, making it possible to apply machine learning models that demand standardized input. We investigated a text normalization technique that utilizes machine learning and text image analysis. The technique entails image embedding for text representation and augmenting the text images to enhance representation quality. Consequently, a transformer model is trained on the transformed images to derive a generalized token embedding. Notably, this token embedding can be applied to different datasets, even those developed after the model's training. The effectiveness of our approach is reflected in the accuracy of part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition on two datasets, despite having no prior experience with those datasets' wordings or token distributions. Additionally, when limited domain data is available, our method can produce a general yet useful token embedding by employing data augmentation. We have made our code available for public use. The results of our study are expected to pave the way for the creation of adaptable, universal language models that can handle text image analysis without prior domain knowledge. These models have the potential to simplify text analysis and extraction across multiple domains, even when domain labels are absent. The outcomes of our study could lead to the development of applicable, generalizable language models. The study demonstrates a tokenization approach that is independent of domain and standardization processes, using data augmentation to create a versatile token embedding that can be applied to any text. The empirical results show that our method is compatible with various text normalization techniques and standardization processes. The study reveals that a tokenization approach and data standardization are intertwined, sharing common components. The results suggest that by leveraging data augmentation, it's possible to create a token embedding that's highly useful even in small datasets. The study showcases the adaptability of transformer models trained on augmented image data for text analysis tasks.
