Link prediction in large knowledge graphs is crucial for maintaining their integrity and scalability. Conventional link scoring methods based on reinforcement learning and message passing often require lengthy training processes, extensive memory, and high computational resources. These challenges hinder the application of these methods to massive knowledge graphs. To overcome these limitations, we developed an innovative approach that leverages static framework development for link forecasting. Our novel technique, known as LinkEcho, employs a pre-trained knowledge graph and fine-tunes a static framework on a subset of training data. This approach avoids the memory demands and high training costs associated with message passing and reinforcement learning methods. Moreover, we developed a novel evaluation metric, End-Adjacent-Population, to assess link forecasting performance and demonstrated the superiority of LinkEcho using knowledge graphs that model temporal information. Our experiments on large knowledge graphs, such as FreeBase and Wikidata, showed that LinkEcho delivers high-quality link forecasting while efficiently utilizing memory and computational resources. Notably, LinkEcho was able to predict around 10 billion links on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, outperforming existing methods by up to 2.5 fold in terms of accuracy. Our study provides valuable insights for adapting link forecasting techniques to large knowledge graphs. The implementation of LinkEcho can be accessed at https://github.com/hse-vertsey/linkecho. Additionally, our results are publicly available at https://vertsey.github.io/linkecho results/. Furthermore, a pre-built Docker image can be found at https://dockerhub.com/hsevertsey/linkecho. An interactive dashboard for link forecasting can be explored at https://linkecho-analysis-browser.vercel.app/loan.struct.html. To facilitate the reproduction of our findings, we have released the linkecho-batch framework, a PyTorch module for batched link forecasting, at https://linkecho-batch.github.io/. The pursuit of high-energy femtosecond lasers remains a central objective, with current methods using Kerr-lens mode-locking in ultrashort pulse lasers being widely applied. A novel analytical approach has been developed to analyze Kerr-lens frequency locking, providing insights into mesoscale phenomena, such as multi-scale pulse broadening and frequency narrowing. By combining the fast and slow axes of the optical cavity, we derive a geometric equation illustrating frequency locking and transform it into a map that predicts Kerr-lens mode-locking in ultrashort pulse lasers. This analytic framework uncovers the underlying dynamics of Kerr-lens mode-locking and highlights its sensitivity to complex nonlinear interactions. We show that parametric modes can emerge from these nonlinear interactions and provide a clear understanding of their contribution to frequency narrowing. We also establish a critical criterion for maintaining single-pulse operation and discuss how to achieve high-energy femtosecond lasers. Finally, we extend our analytical framework to study broadband frequency smoothing and present a novel method for generating clean, broad spectra in ultrashort pulse lasers. We demonstrate that our analytic approach aligns with numerical simulations in the fast-axis perspective, offering a valuable tool for understanding and improving high-energy femtosecond lasers. We apply our framework to a soliton laser and achieve an energy boost of 50 times from 20 nJ to 1000 nJ through mechanical adjustment and careful design of the optical cavity, resulting in increased nonlinearities. This energy increase enables the generation of highly stable, high-coherence pulses with a high signal-to-noise ratio, paving the way for a wide range of scientific and industrial applications. Furthermore, our analytical framework demonstrates that soliton laser generation is not limited to fast-axis nonlinearities and can be applied to a broader range of optical cavities and pump sources, offering exciting possibilities for innovative laser design and optimization. Yet, practical implementations of this approach often run into several challenges, notably, the significant variability in training time, the non-linearity of models, and the unequal accessibility to computational resources across diverse devices. If the imbalance in computational capabilities is not accounted for, some devices might finish training and wait for others to catch up before model updates are shared. This results in inefficient performance and prolonged waiting times for devices with greater processing power. To tackle this issue, we're presenting an innovative method for nonlinear regression that guarantees fair access to updates, takes into consideration computational constraints, and provides an optimal solution in a resource-efficient manner. This method also features a user-friendly robustness guarantee. Through comprehensive testing using artificial datasets, we've shown that our approach not only adheres to the guarantees but also significantly outperforms competing methodologies, notably in scenarios with a high degree of computational disparity. Our findings suggest that the developed technique can successfully integrate diverse datasets and achieve state-of-the-art results. At the same time, the model's size remains manageable, and the method itself is straightforward to execute. This framework can also be applied to a wide array of distributed federated learning applications by modifying the model type and extending the approach accordingly. Additionally, we explore the potential applications of this technology in metric-scale optical resonators and the quantum computing field. We assess nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization 4D formats and propose a novel method for predicting nonlinear distortion. Our approach accounts for the correlation between linear polarization states and reveals that significant nonlinear distortion can occur even with low overall power and high signal-to-nonlinear-distortion power, particularly when the power is unevenly distributed between polarizations. This insight suggests that leveraging polarization's degree of freedom in nonlinear distortion mitigation could be an efficient strategy. Our prediction shows that a dual-polarization system can exhibit distortion similar to that of an equivalent single-polarization system with reduced power by $\sim$3 dB, despite the potential for maximizing this benefit depending on the distribution of power between polarizations. However, if the power between polarizations varies substantially, a modification of our formula may be necessary to obtain accurate results. Our analysis utilizes a approach based on a general nonlinear distortion profile, highlighting the limitation of a widely adopted model that overestimates nonlinear distortion in systems with combined powers and asymmetrical polarization states. Our simulation confirms the validity of our approach and provides a clear understanding of how polarization influences nonlinear distortion. This knowledge can facilitate reflection-free coherence detection, a critical technique for measuring nonlinear distortion, and may also enhance various nonlinear distortion mitigation techniques, such as backward propagation monitoring, pre-compensation, and post-compensation. To demonstrate this, we model a fiber-based transmission system with a spectral efficiency of 6 bits/s/Hz and a total launch power of 5 dB-fiber. Our results show that a backward-post compensation scheme can outperform traditional methods, such as second-order nonlinearity pre-compensation, due to the distinct nonlinear distortion characteristics resulting from polarization's influence. This highlights the potential of leveraging dual-polarization's degrees of freedom to improve nonlinear distortion mitigation. Our work provides a foundation for this goal and inspires future investigations. Our simulation also demonstrates that a backward-post compensation scheme can provide a performance gain of $\sim$1 dB compared to second-order pre-compensation, mainly due to a more accurate model that considers the unique polarization-dependent nonlinear distortion, even when the power between polarizations varies significantly. Our research introduces FIRe-GAN, a groundbreaking approach that employs Generative Adversarial Networks to seamlessly fuse visible and infrared spectra into realistic and high-resolution outputs, focusing on wildfire visualization. This research focuses on the development of a COVID-19 pandemic model through the application of a stochastic continuous-time Markov chain model. The model consists of nine interconnected compartments, which are used to track individuals' states (e.g., healthy, infected, hospitalised) over time. To account for the rapid changes characteristic of pandemics, a linear diffusion term was added to the model, representing random state transitions. To calculate the model parameters, an extensive dataset from the United Kingdom was utilized, involving 393 daily COVID-19 cases from January 23rd to March 23rd, 2021. The model's efficacy is assessed using the Akaike information criterion and the Bayesian information criterion. Following parameter optimization, the model's predictions were compared with actual UK COVID-19 case data, demonstrating relatively accurate predictions for approximately two months after initial data fitting. Notably, an additional three months of data, not utilized in fitting the model, was employed in evaluating predictive performance. Furthermore, the model's outcomes were explored through numerical simulations, which revealed that linear diffusion significantly enhances random state transitions. The model's success highlights its potential as a future COVID-19 case forecast model, especially when no vaccination is available, and could be applied to other rapid epidemic transitions, including those induced by other pathogens. Additionally, considering the ongoing global COVID-19 situation, the model has the potential to be an invaluable tool in public health decision-making for future COVID-19-like outbreaks. The isoscalar giant monopole resonance in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si was studied using the QCD sum rule in combination with the no-core shell model. The examination showed that the isoscalar monopole strength distribution in $^{24}$Mg is dominated by the dynamics of the $sd$ shell, in contrast to $^{28}$Si, where the $sp$ shell plays a significant role, with both cases exhibiting a significant impact of the quadrupole strength distribution. The presence of a positive correlation between the isoscalar monopole and quadrupole strengths leads to a rise in the energy of the isoscalar monopole resonance and potentially causes a reduction in its strength. Theoretical microscopical calculations aligned well with experimental data, thus providing valuable insights into the properties of heavily excited states in nuclei. The method employed in this research may offer a clue for resolving the long-standing issue of the isoscalar monopole resonance in deuterium. The technique developed in this research has the potential to be applied to heavier nuclei. The study demonstrated that the isoscalar monopole resonance in $^{28}$Si has a smaller width compared to $^{24}$Mg, which was not previously observed in theoretical microscopical calculations. The possible explanation for the large width of the isoscalar monopole resonance in $^{24}$Mg through the analysis of its strength distribution reveals that its dynamics is dominated by the $sd$ shell. In a recommender system, understanding the underlying motivation of user actions is crucial for predicting future actions and personalized recommendations will be more effective if tailored to the visible user preferences, which vary depending on the motivation. This study tackles the challenge of identifying a user's hidden motivation, which is their actual goal, a crucial variable in modeling their preferences. We propose a two-component model that extracts both the likelihood of user motivations and the probability of transitioning between different states when the motivation changes. We use an algorithm that simultaneously models both the motivation likelihoods and the transition probabilities between them, based on a user's interaction history. We also introduce a metric that represents how clearly a user's transition probabilities indicate their motivation distribution. We test our model on two datasets and compare it with a baseline model that only models user preferences without considering their motivation. Our results show that our model performs better than the baseline model and that identifying a user's motivation also enhances the performance of a preference model. We also analyze the frequency of different motivation and our model's performance is less affected by changes in user motivation. This study is the first to explore modeling a user's motivation in a recommender system. We demonstrate that our model performs well on a dataset of adult dating and our results imply that a higher degree of user motivation can lead to a better model. We also make our code available for others to use. The model's performance is illustrated through visualization and our analysis reveals new insights such as the popularity of different motivation and how a user's motivation can be identified from their interaction history. Additionally, our model shows that a user's motivation can be used as a new feature to further improve a preference model's performance even if the model does not consider motivation as a feature. We conclude that a user's motivation should be modeled and utilized in a recommender system. We also, for the sake of completeness, provide a baseline model that only models a user's preference without considering their motivation and compare its performance with our model. We show that our model performs better than the baseline model and the difference in their performance can be explained by how well each model considers a user's motivation. We analyze the performance difference and our model's performance suggests that a user's motivation plays a crucial role in a recommender system. Ultimately, our model implies that a user's motivation can be used as a link between a user's visible actions and their underlying preferences, which is essential for a recommender system.

A conceptual framework for distributed regulation is offered as the ideal performance benchmark, even in cases without noise. The open research questions in this area are also identified for potential exploration.

  The performance and stability of a distributed control system are analyzed through a conceptual framework for regulation, even in cases without additive noise.
  A message-passing based distributed filter is presented with strong consistency properties.

  A proof-of-concept example showcases the efficacy of our approaches in a practical application involving wireless sensor networks.
  Additional research questions are proposed to foster advancements in this area.

Through in-depth analysis of this modified model, we identify the distinctive patterns that emerge when considering different timescales. While the original model predicts a stable equilibrium with a single peak for both short and long timescales, we find that an alternative dynamics leads to oscillating solutions within the system's stable region. Our new model is characterized by the interplay between mutation standard deviation and selection intensity, with older, long timescales being governed by standard deviation, while newer, short timescales are influenced by selection intensity. This change affects which modifier, standard deviation or selection intensity, governs ecological dynamics and eventually genetic dynamics. Our results reveal that, regardless of initial conditions, they converge to the same trait value but differ in response to environmental changes, leading to two distinct types of dynamics. When standard deviation dominates, we observe a shift from original to new dynamics, with steady oscillations supressing the peak value of the trait distribution. In seismic imaging, particularily inversion problems, sparse signals are common, with multiple approaches like L1 regularization or sparse SPARSAL methods being employed to take advantage of this phenomenon. However, conventional L1 based regularization methods like L1-regularized optimization or sparse SPARSAL have been shown to be inefficient in non-sparse data environments, leading to poor performance in non-sparsity applications. This article presents a novel learning based method called NuSPAN that utilizes non-uniform sparse data to learn non-uniform penalty weights through a proximal optimization process in a data-driven manner. A provided proof demonstrates that NuSPAN is able to replicate L1 regularization methods' sparse results in uniform sparse environments. In addition, NuSPAN was shown through numerical experiments to be able to learn and represent unique patterns in seismic data from real-world applications. At the core of NuSPAN lies a novel proximal-mean network architecture, where the penalty weights are learned through a data-driven approach, and where the method takes advantage of graph structure to determine the weights. When compared to conventional L1 regularization methods, NuSPAN was shown to produce similar results in uniform sparse environments, while outperforming other methods in non-uniform sparse environments by its ability to accurately replicate the true seismic structure. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA, VMOA, and the α-BMOA. It examines the closedness of such semigroups in a Banach algebra setting and identifies lower and upper bounds, as well as growth and integrability conditions, for the norms of the operators within the semigroup. The study also determines sufficient and necessary criteria for the boundedness of the semigroup in terms of integral functionals, while delving into the relationship between norms and maximal functions associated with these operators. Additionally, it provides equivalent representations of these equivalences in the VMOA setting and offers a characterization of bounded semigroups in BMOA through singular measures. Finally, this article explores the adjointness of certain operator classes on α-BMOA. The study is illustrated with several examples that validate its theoretical findings. By considering the adjointness, it extends various previous results related to Volterra operators on H^p spaces, specifically on the p-BMOA and VMOA/p-BMOA spaces. Moreover, it extends a result of Wallin (1980) concerning integral operators on H^p spaces. The article further researches the adjointness in the setting of α-BMOA for future exploration. The study is completed with an appendix, addressing a problem of the pointwise boundedness of a vector-valued operator from L^2 to BMOA. Specifically, it provides sufficient and necessary criteria for such operator in the form of (LBMOA, L^2, BMOA)-boundedness. The article finally concludes with a discussion on the H^p-boundedness of certain integral operators in the form of (H^p, L^2, BMOA). Although numerous advanced networks have been introduced to improve POS tagging, these methods are often optimized for contemporary languages and may not be effective for historical corpora with different linguistic characteristics. We propose a novel approach to improve POS tagging by utilizing existing models while accounting for potential errors in annotation. A word-level prediction mechanism is designed to assess the likelihood of correct POS tags given a word and the context in which it appears. Experimental results indicate that this approach significantly increases accuracy, improving a state-of-the-art model by 15% in the case of Old French corpora. Recent years have seen escalating demands for powerful feature representation learning in deep models.  A relatively new technique aimed at learning more representative features utilizes vector-basis linear approximation methods such as Taylor series and Newton approximation.  We discover that these methods derivate from a unified framework known as Non-Uniform Integrability (NUI) which blends functional analysis and optimization principles, thus elucidating their underlying mechanism.  By establishing a framework for non-uniformly approximating high-order derivatives of complex functions, we also develop a one-to-one correspondence between NUI and generalized multi-period Investment Theory.  Furthermore, based on the NUI perspective, we develop a novel optimization algorithm known as Non-Uniformly Convergent Gradient (NUG), which generalizes Taylor series and Newton approximation, achieving superior performance in training deep models with sparse features, and even yields new insights into the characteristics of optimization hyper-parameters.  Through rigorous experiments, we validate the effectiveness of NUI in learning more representative features and verify the efficacy of NUG in deep model training.  Ultimately, we apply NUI to the analysis of complex data sequences, thus yielding a deep understanding of investment markets via multi-period investment modeling.  Our research demonstrates that NUI provides a robust mathematical foundation for feature learning and portfolio management.  Specifically, our contributions to the field of feature learning are as follows:  First, we uncover the essential mathematical mechanism behind linear approximation techniques via NUI.  Second, we generalize these methods to accommodate higher-order approximations.  Third, we establish a link between NUI and advanced investment strategies.  Fourth, we develop a new optimization algorithm with superior performance in training deep models with sparse features.  Fifth, and perhaps most importantly, we analyze the impact of optimization hyper-parameters on the performance of deep models.  Sixth, and finally, we leverage NUI to explain the behavior of complex data sequences in finance, thereby shedding new light on portfolio management.  Our research indicates that NUI offers a powerful tool for automatic feature learning and portfolio management without human intervention.  Specifically, our experiments reveal that NUI enables automated discovery of sparse features in datasets, thus accelerating the training process of deep models with fewer requirements for model parameters.  Our research also yields new insights into the impact of optimization hyper-parameters on the performance of deep models as well as the behavior of complex data sequences in finance.  Ultimately, our work delivers a groundbreaking mathematical framework for automatic feature learning and portfolio management.  Our technique generalizes known approximations such as Taylor series and Newton approximation

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its achievements in various multi-modal tasks. Nevertheless, its performance is heavily reliant on high-quality datasets, which can be difficult to obtain, especially in low-resource scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce VT-CLIP, a visual-assisted framework for improving CLIP models without requiring additional labels. By utilizing text-image pairs and permitting early contrasting, VT-CLIP achieves performance gains through visual help in text understanding. We evaluate its effectiveness on multiple datasets, including FLICKR-1M, AID, and the recently released ImageCAPTIONS, demonstrating improved results compared to the original CLIP model and comparable to state-of-the-art outcomes on FLICKR-1M and AID. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that Visual-assisted Contrastive learning is beneficial due to its capacity to speed up convergence and reduce visual-textual drift. We have also released the code and pre-trained models for VT-CLIP at https://github.com/ghuasc/VT-CLIP. An additional experiment is included to address CLIP's class drift issue through VAST-CLIP, as described in the last section. We explore the concept of operator transitioning, which allows us to analyze the computational complexity of noisy matrix frameworks from a higher level, viewed as programs, rather than individual functions. Our work expands on this by exploring three variants of operator transitioning: one that maintains circuit structure, another that allows rearrangement, and a third that allows both rearrangement and module elimination. We demonstrate that these three variants have equivalent decidability and complexity, in turn, demonstrate that the computational complexity of valuing and verifying programs in the noisy matrix framework is equivalent to that of valuing and verifying formulas. Furthermore, we posited the existence of programs (circuits) whose valuing and verifying costs do not match their formula counterparts, which we later confirm for arithmetic circuits. We also investigate the computational complexity of the third variant, showing it to be PSPACE-complete for various noisy matrix frameworks and bounded to be EXPSPACE. Lastly, we investigate the model checking costs of programs (formulas) in the noisy matrix framework, which we find to be PSPACE-complete for circuits and PSPACE-hard for formulas, as well as demonstrating that the model checking costs of programs and formulas do not always align with each other. While digital encoding has long been utilized, its potential for enhancing interoperability between systems remains underrealized due to the absence of industry-standard guidelines and widely adopted software that follows those guidelines. We aim to fill this void by introducing highdicom, a Python framework that leverages DICOM for the standardized encoding of image-based annotations and machine learning outputs, along with providing example use cases. This user-friendly library offers built-in support for the most commonly employed image analysis methods, allowing users to generate compliant files quickly and access pre-built templates for high-detailed analyses. By promoting the adoption of highdicom, we hope to contribute to the development of a shared understanding within the digital pathology and radiology community, ultimately leading to the establishment of a standardized data exchange framework. This early release of highdicom seeks to gather feedback from users and researchers to refine and enhance its functionality, with the final version expected to adhere strictly to industry standards, thereby ensuring that its benefits are long-lasting and not compromised in the near future. The conversion to a more conservative approach will be highlighted by several examples of highdicom's most useful features. Highdicom is now publicly available on GitHub's open-source platform at https://github.com/ITINER/higdicom, where users can contribute new functionality and collaborate in the development of a more sustainable, open-standards based future. Specifically, this approach offers a method for converting Poisson maps into symplectic maps, which provides an alternative method for clebsch integration. However, this method's connection to a broader geometric framework was unclear. Here, we establish that certain Lie-Poisson systems can be authorized by geometric data on a level set of momentum maps, which includes properties such as non-degeneracy and co-isotropy. We demonstrate that these momentum maps, which are subject to specific constraints, map symplectic forms, which leads to a broader geometric interpretation of the method for integrating Lie-Poisson systems, and also serves as a method for left invariant integration on certain types of geometric structures associated with quantum groups. We apply this method to a variety of illustrative examples and re-derive known results in order to showcase its scope and potential. Furthermore, this method also allows us to conclude that the left kinematic symmetry of the q-gaussian probability density corresponds to a non-chiral, $SU_2$-moment map that is non-degenerate and co-isotropic. We also show that this result has significant implications for both the quantum group and geometric statistical inference contexts. Specifically, we demonstrate that the left kinematic symmetry of the q-gaussian corresponds to a certain type of maximal non-degenerate symplectic action, which indicates that the q-gaussian has reached its maximum under left kinematic symmetry. We apply this result in the quantum group context and conclude that the exponents of the CG-coefficients of the $SU_2($q$\otimes q$)$-representation possess a common denominator, which equals the level of the quantum group. Furthermore, we also conclude that the exponents of the CG-coefficients of the $SU_2($q$\otimes q$)$-representation equal the dual levels of the group actions defined by the geometric data on a level set of momentum maps, which includes properties such as non-degeneracy and co-isotropy. We also show that these exponents are expressed as certain Casimirs of the group $SU_2($\bar q$\otimes q$)$, which implies that they equal zero. While convolutions are foundational in computer vision, their orientation-limited nature leads to some information being overlooked, such as edge direction. One solution, the orientation convolve network, addresses this by introducing a new layer that combines conventional convolution and a deconvolution process, allowing for variable orientation. This makes it the first fully rotational invariant convolution type where the number of parameters does not increase with orientation variations. Experimentation shows OCN results to be on par with state-of-the-art for image classification on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. However, a notable decrease in performance was observed when orientation was fully varied, highlighting OCN's strength in cases with limited orientation variability. Further benefits of this approach include its reduced parameter count, lower FLOPs, and greater adaptability. An exploration of applying OCN to other areas of computer vision is also proposed. 

Following the initial publication of this paper, a more detailed description of the orientation convolve layer, including its mathematical representation, was added, along with a study comparing its performance to other proposed methods in high orientation variability scenarios. The updated results demonstrate OCN's lower accuracy but comparable parameter, Flops, and latency costs when compared to the best-in-class approach in this scenario. This insight suggests that the initial paper presented an oversimplified experiment where the orientation variability was fixed at 90 degrees, while in reality more variable orientations could lead to enhanced performance.

A thorough examination of the relationship between energy, mass, and temperature in a system with multiple particles reveals an intriguing property - a unique combination of energy and mass can be replicated by various configurations of the system's momentum and mass distributions. Consequently, a system with a significant amount of particles can have multiple energy-mass combinations, which can be observed at high energy levels. A detailed example demonstrates that, in a system with a large number of particles, a linear relationship between energy and mass may not be sufficient to determine the system's characteristics uniquely, necessitating a more comprehensive analysis. We establish a Ventla-Kato hypercontractive inequality for specific Fock spaces weighted by functions that increase polynomially, as well as unweighted Berman spaces, and extend this inequality to operators representing quadratic combinations of position and momentum. The proof primarily relies on resolving an $L^p$ estimate for which the solution was previously provided in arXiv:2101.05214. Building upon this estimate, we adapt the approach of Griesemer and Sjoestrand to derive the desired inequalities. In the process, we also prove the reverse Faber-Krahn inequality in the context of Berman spaces. Furthermore, we extend the inequality to scenarios where the weight functions vary with time, providing examples of the implications, which notably include the emergence of "light-cone combinations" of position and momentum. The latter phenomenon was previously observed in the context of Klein-Gordon equations by Sjoestrand in arXiv:2101.05214. The approach used in this article can be adapted to other operator types, such as those representing timewise increasing weights or position operators with time-dependent weights. It can also be applied to second quantized versions of these operators, with the latter relevant in the context of recent work, arXiv:2101.05214. However, when dealing with time-based increases in weights, the problem turns out to be significantly more complex, leading to the need for new ideas not required in the other two scenarios. In particular, to establish the hypercontractive inequality for timewise increasing weights, we require both an $L^p$ estimate resolution and an analysis of the operator's kernel. The latter is inherently simpler than the first contribution in this article. The time-based weight case was initially explored in the author's thesis, with a revised version presented under the title "Hypercontractivity for timewise weighted Berman spaces and Berezin estimates". The approach used in this article can be applied to operators representing quadratic combinations of position and momentum, as well as second quantized versions of these operators, for both position-based and momentum-based increasing weights, except for perfect increasing weights, which were initially solved in the author's thesis, with a revised version presented under the title "Perfect weights in second quantization of Berman spaces". Active learning strategies that use queries to identify uncertain model predictions rely on uniform uncertainty across space to minimize the need for expensive annotations. However, in cases where data is locally clustered, uniform uncertainty may not be easily achieved. New approaches, such as regional queries, address this issue by targeting areas of higher uncertainty. But, has learning resiliently, especially in the face of out-of-distribution challenges, been prioritized over accuracy? We evaluated the effect of regional queries on uncertainty reduction and out-of-distribution performance. Surprisingly, regional queries boosted residual uncertainty but hindered accuracy-based uncertainty reduction. Moreover, while regional queries improved performance on OOD tasks, they did so by exacerbating class-based uncertainty rather than confidence-based uncertainty and led to poorer calibration. We found top-performing regional queries lack a governing principle and may offer opportunities for future research. Ultimately, using regional queries without baseline comparisons is ill-advised and may hamper model performance in the end. Furthermore, users reported the robotic system to be easy to operate and offered clear visual representations of the scan in real-time. This study supports the use of robotic ultrasound imaging for scoliosis evaluation due to its high reliability and ease of use, with the added benefit of precise repetitive measurements that can lead to increased accuracy and objectivity. This research introduces a technique for expanding or shortening speech at the segmental level. Unlike prior methods, our approach doesn't rely on probability models and instead utilizes a dynamic programming framework to identify optimal subsequence medians for inserting or removing segments. A median-based sequence is then created by replacing original sequence values with these medians, ensuring that the modified sequence's segmental medians match the desired length. To preserve natural variations, we integrate our algorithm with a variant of the Vector Quantization technique, allowing our method to outperform existing techniques in terms of chunkiness. Furthermore, we have developed an efficient memory-based linear spectral transformation algorithm, which achieves lower frequency warping artifacts in comparison to prior methods. The results of our experiments are promising, suggesting a median-driven length adjustment can be an effective and high-quality alternative. In modern deep convolutional neural networks, a popular approach called Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) is used for efficient parameter sharing. It was found, however, that concurrent sharing of weights and interactions for different input channels can be ineffective and leads to shared weights that lack consistency in their parameters. This leads to suboptimal performance and confusion over the shared weights, particularly when dealing with various inputs. This paper presents a Simple Feature Sharing (SFS) framework that streamlines parameter sharing through a unique normalization process, ensuring equalization of weights for distinct inputs at each layer. This equalsized distribution of weights ensures optimal extraction of relevant features from each input, and their fusion yields enhanced performance, particularly when cross-modal interactions are involved. Equalization also enables decoupling of cross-modal interactions and identification of their significance. Equalized features can be further refined through modulation or other operations before being combined. This framework's versatility allows its equalization process to be tightened or loosened according to specific requirements. Experiments with datasets such as Modality Mix, PADCAN-051, and PROSTATE have demonstrated that using SFS outperforms existing methods such as early fusion and hypertensor ranking for feature extraction. Furthermore, analysis of SFS's performance during training and deployment has shown its potential to create enhanced multi-modal pipelines that outperform current methods, and serve as a more effective prior for designing MIMO structures. A new structure is established called an authority framework, adapted from directed graphs applied to directed spaces. Authorities act as a set of preferred locations, with movements weighted relative to their distance, capturing the concept of authority locations being more attractive upon reaching them. We investigate the geometric properties of this metric, defining a path-weighted metric $\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(x, y)$ that quantifies the attractiveness of a path between two locations $x$ and $y$. We define a new space property called path-monusity, characterize the relationship between this property and the existence of authorities, and explore the relationship between $\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(x, y)$ and more general metrics. Additionally, the notion of semi-metric authority frameworks is defined and examined in the context of directed spaces. We establish conditions under which semi-metric authority frameworks can be embedded into metric authority frameworks, and illustrate a metric authority framework on the set of positive defined measures equipped with the Wasserstein distance. We define a new mathematical object called an authority path, establish its correspondence with traditional paths, and investigate its applications, particularly in developing a Mincovski inequality akin to a Szolgi inequality in Gromov's hyperbolicity theory. We define a new inequality of authority path type, $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A}}(x, y)$, and demonstrate its relationship with the visibility, hyperbolicity, and geodesic core properties of directed spaces. We show that a directed space is geodesically core if and only if $\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A}}(x, y)$ holds for all $x, y$ in the space. We define a new inequality of path-type, path-visibility, and demonstrate its relationship with the core property. We establish the path-visibility inequality as an optimization criterion for an authority framework. We define a new inequality of semi-metric authority framework type, semi-Vis-$\mathcal{A}$, and demonstrate its relationship with the core property. We establish semi-Vis-$\mathcal{A}$ as an optimization criterion for a semi-metric authority framework. The analysis focuses on the Sahara Desert and a coastal area of Chile, observing precipitation patterns over a 30-year period. Our research introduces the Bayesian Statistics Directed Label Renovation Mechanism (BDRM), specifically designed to counterbalance the phenomenon of label noise prevalent in datasets utilized for supervised learning. By incorporating the Bayesian framework and incorporating a mechanism to update existing labels, BDRM aims to enhance the model's resistance to label noise. This approach, a variation of the DRNM method, is tested on challenging categorical image datasets including one medical image dataset, where it demonstrates comparable performance or superior performance compared to existing methods such as label regularization, noise-aware loss functions, and current data rectification mechanisms. This algorithm can be applied to a broad spectrum of supervised learning models without needing modifications to the underlying code. Furthermore, BDRM directs labeling towards more valuable applications by identifying high fidelity samples and labeling them, while assigning a smaller priority to labeling less confident examples. This paper introduces an novel polynomial expression for the transition probability matrix of a random walk related to a graph with vertex degrees $d_i$, starting from a given state $i$. When the random walk is described using a simple random walk, we can determine if the transition probability matrix satisfies the polynomial expression by checking a specific set of conditions. These conditions are associated with the eigenvalues of the matrix and involve relationships between its irreducible components. In the context of a graph that is connected in general, but not necessarily connected, we can establish unique polynomial expressions for the transition probability matrices of each irreducible component. Additionally, we can verify that our polynomial expressions are distinctive, meaning no generic matrix polynomial can encompass the variation of transition probability matrices across all possible graphs of the same size. Our analysis is based on the irreducibility of the graph and its components, as well as the specific properties associated with the eigenvalues of the transition probability matrices. In particular, we demonstrate that for a graph that is not generally connected, the constant term of the polynomial expression for the transition probability matrix of each irreducible component is equal to 0. This result extends to the scenario where the random walk is non-reversible. Our study is focused on identifying polynomial expressions for the transition probability matrices of random walks, but these findings are equally applicable to other contexts, such as Markov chains. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for using polynomial expressions to solve specific problems related to graphs, such as inverse hidden Markov models. To validate our analysis, we provide demonstration examples featuring the polynomial expressions for the transition probability matrices of random walks. In formal reasoning, definitions play a pivotal role, influencing both the structure and content of proofs, and often, if a definition proves problematic, reconsidering the approach can be challenging. A newly introduced, timed aspect in the HOL definition process is studied here, with the argument put forth that it rarely yields unambiguous interpretations. Rather, unintended interpretations often arise due to an insufficiently calibrated timeline. This paper seeks to establish a framework of principles governing timed definitions, providing a clear and precise definition without introducing additional assumptions, and examining its implications in a context where events occur concurrently. It is further demonstrated how the approach can be applied to resolve usability issues observed in a previous definition of laconic predicates for elementary numbers. Silicene, a single layer of silicon atoms, exhibits electrons that behave unlike those in silicon and exhibit piezoelectric properties. Despite its promising properties, silicene typically decomposes when attempted on conventional substrates. In contrast, hexagonal boron nitride shows promise as a stable substrate. Our investigation involves analyzing silicene layered on hexagonal boron nitride using high-throughput computational methods. Results indicate that the boron nitride substrate stabilizes the silicene layer and influences the properties of nearby manganese atoms. These findings may facilitate experimental researchers in understanding and interpreting their data. Additionally, we demonstrate a procedure for calculating and mapping the spin-polarization of individual atoms, offering potential in silicene-based spintronics applications. Furthermore, we explore the electronic interactions between the manganese atoms, and discuss possible approaches for producing and utilizing these interactions. We also investigate the electronic interactions between the manganese atoms and learn that they can stabilize on boron nitride with hexagonal coordination, but with a manganese dopant concentration of 25%. This concentration produces a collective phenomenon known as ferromagnetism. These interactions consist of a quantum phenomenon known as exchange and van der Waals forces that may facilitate novel phenomena when combined with the physics of multiple states or quantum fluctuations. The ferromagnetic state and quantum fluctuations can be stabilized at a manganese dopage concentration of 25% through molecular adsorption or at concentrations of 33% through intentional doping, however these concentrations can also result in an anti-ferromagnetic state due to an alternative explanation for the data. Possible applications of these interactions and novel phenomena include the production of advanced quantum computers, quantum simulators, and novel transistors, as well as unexpected phenomena for those interested in studying and exploring them. These results could be experimentally produced by placing a few atomic layers of manganese on boron nitride with an ultra-low temperature to reduce the amount of manganese to 25% or by intentionally doping a few atomic layers onto silicene to result in a uniform and stable 25% coverage. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to detect nuclear recoils independently from electron recoils, particularly in dark matter searches, is crucial with gaseous detectors. This involves selecting and utilizing suitable events that recoil both electrons and nuclei. We introduce two new observables that can directly identify both signal and background interactions in a single detector. We demonstrate their effectiveness using simulated interactions in a single-photocathode detector and showcase their potential to optimize existing detectors for improved sensitivity. These new observables have the potential to be applied to various detectors, including those used in direct detection experiments, such as the MAAS under construction. We also explore their compatibility with existing detection methods based on ionization signals. By comparing simulated interactions in a superconducting detector, we highlight the advantages of using these new observables to distinguish signal quarks from background quarks in the quadrature plot without requiring additional detection methods. We propose to apply this technique in existing detectors, including XENONN, CRESST, and MAAS, with the goal of improving their sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles. Furthermore, we aim to adapt this technique for experimental search on existing detectors, including EDELWEISS, DMX, and the future EUREKA experiment. Studies have shown that implementing this technique can significantly reduce background interference in existing detectors. We also plan to apply this technique for simultaneous analysis of various processes between electrons and nuclei, and between alpha particles and nuclei, which will be particularly useful in future large-scale MAAS detectors to extract more accurate data. Finally, we have obtained relevant technical specifications for building and testing the MAAS detector at SLAC, including laboratory setup and experimental procedures. The results of our simulations suggest that it is feasible to achieve a detection rate of one interaction per day at a 95% confidence level. We plan to analyze data using the MAAS experiment at SLAC in 2023. The outcome of our simulation indicates that it is possible to lower background interference, demonstrating the potential benefits of this technique. We also plan to establish two new datasets, one including signal events from both electrons and nuclei and another comprising single-scatter events. By using these new datasets, the MAAS experiment at SLAC in 2023 will be able to achieve sensitivity at a 95% confidence level of $2 \times 10^{-10}$ in June 2023. In various safety-critical domains like commercial driving, AI-driven decision support systems must demonstrate robust capability in identifying critical events, even in diverse operational environments and conditions. However, technological limitations prevent the widespread adoption of AI systems in everyday commercial vehicle settings. To overcome this challenge, experts can supervise AI system performance on real-world data, but this process faces its own set of difficulties, especially in domains like commercial driving where expert-driven feedback is fragmented and dispersed across various locations. This fragmentated feedback hinders the effectiveness of supervised learning, making it difficult to implement uniformly across different commercial vehicle domains. To address this issue, we propose the creation of a centralized 'expert bus' that facilitates the collection, prioritization, and synchronization of feedback from multiple sources, thus enhancing the consistency of supervised learning across various domains. The proposed 'expert bus' system has far-reaching implications for not only commercial driving but also any setting requiring the integration of human expertise into machine learning. Our method was tested in a study evaluating the effectiveness of commercial drivers in detecting critical events, and our findings highlight the importance of expert collaboration enabled by the 'expert bus', especially when the underlying distribution of event data is complex. Moreover, by utilizing complex data distributions, we examined the efficacy of our approach in identifying event patterns and establishing relationships between them. This research not only contributes to the field of commercial driving, but its methods and insights can also benefit a broader range of applications where human expertise and machine learning intersect. Ultimately, by leveraging the 'expert bus', collaborations between human experts can be unified, enabling the collective advancement of machine learning and bridging the existing gaps in AI system performance, especially in high-stakes domains like commercial driving. The proposed idea is substantiated through a study demonstrating the efficacy of expert supervision in the commercial driving setting. Moreover, by using the 'expert bus' to centralize diverse feedback, our research can potentially address challenges in machine learning and expert supervision more broadly. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents a significant breakthrough in the integration of human expertise into machine learning. The transport properties of armchair graphene nanostructures in the presence of external magnetic fields and spin-orbit interactions are investigated using Green's functions. A general expression is derived for the conductance using tight-binding model Hamiltonians, and this is applied to a pair of coupled nanoribbons to study their transport behavior. It is found that the conductance oscillates in response to changing magnetic field strength due to Bloch states' band structure variations, and that this phenomenon is amplified in longer nanostructures. Introducing spin-orbit interactions causes the conductance to exhibit a Hall-type pattern as a result of the altered band structures, and this effect can be manipulated by controlling the geometry of the nanostructures to enhance or suppress the response. Furthermore, it is discovered that magnetization can be induced within the nanostructure by adjusting its shape, and that transport properties and magnetism are closely linked through the exchange interaction, and can be controlled by varying the magnetic field and nanostructure dimensions. These findings demonstrate that magnetic fields play a crucial role in the transport and magnetic properties of graphene nanostructures that exhibit ferromagnetic ordering. Such control over magnetism could potentially be used in the development of spintronics based on these structures. However, when a similar analysis is conducted for edge-oriented graphene nanostructures, it is found that their transport and magnetic properties exhibit entirely different patterns of behavior, illustrating that these phenomena depend heavily on the specific geometry of the graphene-based systems under investigation. The adaptive spectral Koopman technique has the capability to reconstruct complex nonlinear system behaviors using a limited number of data observations. This involves projecting the dynamics onto a finite-dimensional coordinate system for analysis. Nevertheless, dealing with global properties across all possible coordinates can be impractical, as it may lead to overfitting. On the other hand, focusing solely on essential system features is challenging when the underlying dynamics are unknown. To address these issues, the proposed approach combines the adaptive spectral Koopman technique with sparse-grid techniques to analyze tensor data, effectively reducing the gap between model-based predictive methods and data-driven approaches. This allows for a dynamic balance between exploration and persistence by projecting data onto optimized, adaptively-selected coordinates. Through numerical simulations on both simple systems and complex turbulence data, the proposed approach demonstrates improved efficiency and accuracy compared to traditional spectral methods, particularly for identifying multiple equilibrium states. Additionally, the proposed approach has potential applications in a variety of areas such as weather, combustion, and turbulence, where solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations is often a difficult task. Global cities serve as key economic engines, with high-density urban living offering unparalleled cultural, social, and economic benefits. However, the COVID-19 pandemic brought severe metropolis disruptions, prompting governments to impose strict movement restrictions. The recovery process relied heavily on the resilience of urban service industries and transportation systems, as cities readjusted to prioritize public health over economic activity. The pandemic served as a turning point for reevaluating urban planning considerations, with an urgent need for assessing how urban environments affect quality of life and how individual well-being impacts interaction with the built environment. The unprecedented pandemic response provided an opportunity for analytical insight into the complex relationships between individual behavior, urban environments, and public health policies. Our study utilizes a data-driven, agent-based approach to simulate pedestrian interactions in major cities worldwide under pre-pandemic and pandemic conditions. The analysis is based on a publicly available dataset of daily transaction records in Manhattan, New York City from 2014 to 2015. The findings indicate that the pandemic significantly altered pedestrian behavior in the early stages of the outbreak, with an unexpected shift from lower-density crowds to denser conditions in later stages, seemingly driven by participants' changing behavior in response to their perceived financial gains. The underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon reveal that individuals prioritized locations closest to their homes and essential services, while also demonstrating an increased propensity for traveling longer distances in later stages of the pandemic. The disparity in urban interactions was found to be exacerbated during the pandemic, with individuals from lower-income areas displaying reduced mobility and increased concentration in lower-density areas, underscoring a persistent inequity in access to public services and urban amenities. The underlying financial incentives underlying pedestrian behavior have significant implications for urban planning, particularly in designing pandemic-resilient urban systems that can withstand future crises. The study's findings serve as a call to action for urban policymakers to prioritize and implement intelligent design strategies for recovering from the pandemic, with an emphasis on maintaining social distancing norms and promoting financial equality in urban interactions. The intersection of unidirectional chiral metamaterials and optical cavities holds significant promise for advancing optical science and technology, but due to inherent bidirectional properties, traditional chiral structures are ill-suited for achieving true unidirectional propagation of light. Conversely, we propose a novel optical cavity based on a unilateral chiral medium, where the wave propagation is exclusively one-way and aligned with one of the chiral unit vector's possible orientations. This innovative design results in optical wave polarization being completely modified after a specific distance, giving rise to a unique scenario where the wave exhibits two-fold unpolarized behavior upon traveling a distance that is an odd multiple of the fundamental propagation length. We have successfully built such an optical cavity and demonstrated the predicted one-way chiral propagation of light. This groundbreaking finding opens up uncharted territory in the realm of unidirectional optical cavities and nano-photonics, potentially enabling the development of secure quantum communication networks and advanced light-based technologies. Moreover, we have identified a range of exciting applications in optical nano-imaging, bio-imaging, and detection, and have even discovered the possibility of harnessing the chiral cavity to detect extremely rare and homogeneous chiral molecular enantiomers. Our study thus explores the fascinating interface between one-way propagation and optical polarization, and offers a wealth of exciting avenues for exploring chiral optical phenomena. Ultimately, we anticipate these findings and the resulting technologies to hold a significant place in the forefront of current research and future innovation in the field of optical science and technology. The research presented in this report has far-reaching implications and provides a solid foundation for future work in the field of optical nano-photonics and nano-optics. TERS is an emerging technique that offers unparalleled insight into the electronic and geometric properties of nanomaterials. This method relies on the interaction between a near field microscope and nanostructured scatterers to reveal the underlying chemistry and electromagnetic properties of materials at the nanoscale. Current explanations for TERS images and spectra rely on the semi-classical principle, but we have developed a full quantum mechanical model that enables simulation of the technique. This approach includes calculations of the technique's active space defined by the interacting aperture and sample groups, as well as the role of image charges and their implications. Our results indicate that the hyperconjugative effect plays a significant role in the interpretation of NERS and TERS spectra. This effect provides a concise framework for understanding the relative intensities of spectra based on the relative importance of different influences. The quantum mechanical model offers a theoretical foundation for understanding the underlying mechanisms of TERS and identifying new applications for the technique, including its potential use in the analysis of transition metal dichalcogenides. This model also highlights areas where the technique falls short, providing valuable insights into regions where the technique's signal strength is limited. This work establishes a new understanding of the principles governing TERS and opens up new avenues for investigation and analysis. The method's implementation in the quantum chemistry package Psi will facilitate its adoption by researchers, providing access to a wide range of parameters and adjustments that can be tailored to suit specific study designs. This approach to TERS offers a unique perspective on its capabilities and limitations, allowing for the optimization of conditions for the production of high-quality data. Additionally, the computation of second derivatives and diagonalization of the Hessian matrix in the analysis confirm that the influences responsible for the unique electromagnetic properties of the technique are rooted in the hyperconjugative effect. This effect emerges as a quantum mechanical phenomenon that is absent in classical theories. The theoretical framework of the quantum mechanical model is grounded in the principles of quantum chemistry, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding the underlying mechanisms of TERS. Specifically, the method predicts that the most influential electromagnetic influences are lowest in energy and have s-type symmetry, providing a concise theoretical framework for their interpretation. This approach to TERS offers a level of insight into the geometric properties of the interaction that is absent in classical theories. As robots increasingly work alongside people in varied settings, it's essential for humans be able to instruct these robots in everyday language. We investigate how people perceive and anticipate the actions of a robot assisting with a task, particularly when instructed to a single degree of freedom. Through a series of studies involving a large number of participants, we discovered that people establish expectations for a task's parameters, such as angle and distance, but are ambiguous about tasks involving relative positions. We demonstrate that humans establish more accurate expectations for angular than for radial guidance, and that prior experience with an assisting robot conveys more information than prior experience with an automated system. We also found that explicit warnings about uncertainty conveys little information and that overconfidence in a robot's capabilities leads to higher expectations for successful completion of a task, even when the associated costs are revealed. These findings have implications for the design of interfaces where humans interact with robots and decide the course of action for collaborative tasks. We discuss how this conveys information in various scenarios including a 5 DoF robot assisting in a package delivery scenario. Our research suggests interfaces that induce ambiguity and take advantage of a uncertainty principle can be used to enable safe and efficient interactions when robots work alongside people in a variety of environments. We demonstrate that interfaces which ask people to indicate the direction of an action convey the actions intentions in a manner similar to those interfaces which ask people to specify the distance of an action. We showcase the effectiveness of these conveys information interfaces in a 5 DoF scenario through a donation experiment where a donation is provided when the robot understands the user's instructions and the user trusts the robot's capabilities to execute those instructions. We also implement these conveys information interfaces in a 7 DoF manipulation scenario through a continuation experiment and demonstrate that interfaces which induce uncertainty in actions with many DoF can be used to represent the object's spatial structure that is not visible to either the human or the robot. Our object level experiments have the potential to greatly impact a variety of donating scenarios where a donation is provided when the robot and the user execute a plan as a team. For tasks like delivery or maintenance work, knowing the layout of the area you're navigating is crucial, but maps aren't always available or completely reliable. Existing solutions focus on task-specific cases or rely on repetitive training data patterns. We're taking a different approach with HiTMap, a flexible map representation method that learns to navigate unknown environments using just a few global observations, without relying on pre-planned routes or assuming environmental consistency. Instead, HiTMap builds upon partial reward observations from autonomous agents while adjusting for biased navigation cues. We demonstrate HiTMap's effectiveness in simulated maintenance scenarios and show its ability to learn and adapt from experience in real-world scenarios, just like a new employee would. Compared to other methods, HiTMap achieves similar learning efficiency in about half the number of steps, while also reducing reward losses by two-thirds. Furthermore, HiTMap learns to navigate safely without any data preparation and successfully completes challenging simulations like maintaining robots, where it not only detects when it's lost but also adjusts its navigation when the environment changes or finds new routes to its destination. Overall, HiTMap offers a promising answer to the challenge of navigating unfamiliar environments with minimal data and pre-planning. You can access the code for HiTMap at https://github.com/sjgorman/HiTMap. This paper presents two novel digital sequence code sets derived from multivariable functions.  The first code set known as 2-D (m+n) multi-group code set was developed using a different order multi-group multi-variate function, while the second code set known as 2-D z-complementary array code set was developed using a unified multivariable function.  The paper provides the theoretical foundations for these novel code sets along with the algorithms for their automatic creation. An example is provided to illustrate the creation process of these novel code sets.  The proposed code sets have the potential to enhance the performance of digital communication systems in terms of sequence cross-correlation properties which in turn could lead to system improvements such as increased data transfer rates, improved error detection capabilities and system energy efficiency. Furthermore, this approach is not only limited to digital communication systems but can also be applied in other related fields.  The paper concludes by outlining several potential applications of these novel code sets. Additionally, an online tool has been created where users can input parameters such as the size of the code set and other variables to generate the corresponding codes automatically.  The tool is known as the '2-D Digital Sequence Code Set Generator Tool' and can be accessed using the following URL: https://ceng.ucf.edu/~msameer/2DseqSetGenerator.html. The corresponding codes can be further optimized using the algorithms presented in a related paper titled 'Optimization Techniques for 2-D Digital Sequence Code Sets' also published in this conference. We investigate how electron'spill-over' and nonlocality affect the propagation of surface plasmons across ultra-small gaps between two metal spheres held at a constant charge, connected via an electron reservoir. By employing Thomas-Fermi approximation and a refined screened Thomas-Fermi approximation for nonlocal calculations, we derive closed-form equations of motion for surface plasmons and compare them to a model based on a single fermionic mode. Notably, in the context of quantum dots, the predicted plasmon linewidths exceed those predicted by a simple particle-in-a-box model significantly, highlighting the importance of nonlocal screening and spill-over effects. These phenomena emerge due to a failure in Thomas-Fermi approximation to conserve total electron charge, resulting in energy shifts that are proportional to nonlocal screening frequencies and plasmon energies. Furthermore, in the context of quantum dots, these charge shifts outweigh the decoherence effect, offering scope for realising quantum-resistant calculations. Lastly, in the limit of vanishing gaps, nonlocal screening significantly impacts surface plasmon dispersion, displaying an asymptotic relation to $\sqrt{\nu}$, rendering the phase velocity reusable and revealing a failure in Thomas-Fermi approximation to recover classical electrostatics in this limit. These charge corrections and dispersion changes unveil a deeper connection between classical electrostatics and fermionic nonlocal screening effects. Overall, in the context of quantum optics, these charge and dispersion corrections can be interpreted as quantum versions of optical dispersion and can be used to recover classical optics in the limit of high frequencies. Additionally, in the context of quantum information, these corrections may be utilized as a quantum bit for reading out information from quantum computers. Importantly, these nonlocal screening effects may be utilized as a basis for quantum-resistant cryptography since a breach in Thomas-Fermi approximation leads to a significant shift in surface plasmon resonance, enabling the detection of the breach via plasmon-mediated absorption, transmissivity, or scattering signals. Such a breach can be caused by either a third party or a Coherent Vibrational Mode (CVM) that couples to surface plasmons via plasmon-matter coupling, offering a quantum-compatible approach for the assessment and verification of quantum-resistant properties. Moreover, in the context of quantum information, these electron'spill-over' effects can be exploited as an essential resource for the implementation of quantum distributed processing and distributed information. Importantly, these Plasmon-Assisted Quantum Distributions (PAQD) offer a promising approach for the assessment and verification

To accelerate research in this area, we establish a set of fundamental requirements for designing interactive tools that process multiple-related sequences. These standards include fast and precise comparisons of data points, seamless navigation across related sequences, and intuitive visualization of sequential information. Based on these principles, we propose the MultiSeqVis framework, a comprehensive set of visual representations for illustrating sequences, comparing data points, and connecting related sequences. Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), a technique that requires a fair representation of the environment to prevent bias towards specific vehicle designs or features. However, advances in aperture sensors such as cameras and LiDARs introduce variations in sensor data, leading to inconsistencies in map generation and pose estimation. Furthermore, historical data from past experiences can also be leveraged to improve accuracy, though it poses a risk of introducing prejudice if not properly regulated. This research aims to address this issue by developing a method to eliminate prejudice from distribution-to-distribution map generation. Our approach involves utilizing a deep neural network (DNN) filter inspired by signal processing principles to balance historical data against current sensor inputs, ensuring that the resulting map remains free from bias. Through simulation testing within a diverse urban setting, we validate that our approach effectively mitigates prejudice and maintains accurate localization, while also revealing areas for further improvement. Our code is publicly available for further development. Our study demonstrates that distributing knowledge globally can be beneficial, yet also emphasize the importance of addressing variations in sensor data and accounting for the potential spread of biased information. Our approach can be adapted to tackle prejudice in various fields, from computer vision to natural language processing. Our study contributes a novel DNN filter to address prejudice, while highlighting a thought-provoking use case that could shape the future of information distribution in autonomous systems. Our approach may inspire researchers to tackle prejudice in their own areas of expertise. Our framework can guide researchers to address prejudice in simultaneous localization and mapping, representing a significant breakthrough. In the translation process, interpreters often look ahead to several sentences when determining a single phrase's meaning, yet previous studies have focused primarily on analyzing context in a retrospective manner. To mimic this forward-thinking approach, we've developed a new translator component, the Look-forward Attention module, which considers relationships between a sentence's future and past. We've integrated this module into two existing translators: the Transformer and NMT-ML. Through extensive testing on the IWSLT 14 German-English and WMT19 English-German datasets, we've demonstrated that combining the Look-forward Attention with these translators enhances their translation accuracy. Notably, when paired with the Transformer, the Look-forward Attention module resulted in nearly 2.7 and 1.1 percentage points of improvement in terms of BLEU score on the IWSLT15 and 2019 datasets, respectively. Moreover, a comparative analysis of our Look-forward Attention module and existing Attention and Attention-without-aggregation modules reveals that it leads to lower average and standard deviations of the token-wise log-likelihood in the out-of-vocabulary cases. To visualize these comparisons, we've created a regionmap. The proposed Look-forward Attention module is available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/cyangil/Look-forward-Attention. The experiment's results can be accessed at https://cyangil.github.com/Look-forward-Attention. The module's implementations of Transformer and NMT-ML are available at https://github.com/cyangil/Transformer-NMT-ML. The dataset used can be accessed at https://www.statmt.org/IWSLT2015/. To mitigate domain shift, we've followed our cross-domain adaptation strategy, which is described in our previous research at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10488. Our method does not require any specific data and can rely solely on the translated text following the original distribution, which is achieved using our data acquisition strategy at https://github.com/cyangil/data-acquisition-for-domain-shift. The involved parameters are described in our research at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10488. To evaluate our method, we've conducted our generalization test using our metrics, the Generalization Metrics, which are available at https://github.com/cyangil/generalization-metrics. Our analysis shows that our method enhances both translation accuracy and its forward-looking nature. This signature differs from the patterns generated by the standard cosmic microwave background (CMB) features produced by the cosmic string network. In addition to these periodic features, features related to primal features and the cosmic scale can be used, which are distinct from the scales associated with the CMB features. Moreover, these early features are a natural fit for the explanation of the observed Hubble tension as they influence the scale of their generation and impact the early cosmology in a noticeable fashion during the radiation-dominated era. The theory is also expanded to consider multiple primal features and their interactions with new particles in a setting analogous to particle collider experiments. This could potentially reveal the properties of these early features through an analog particle physics analysis of the primordial universe. The proposed features are most visible in a range of energies between 10^9 and 10^12 GeV and could be further studied with planned experiments to probe the primordial universe at these energy levels and beyond. These future missions include the PRISM, JAXA's NGMS, and ESA's PUMA space missions. This research offers a fresh perspective on explaining observed primordial features and signals through a creative application of cosmological collider physics. Understanding how deep neural networks operate for visual tasks like image classification is a top research priority, despite significant challenges in decoding the structure of these complex models. Recent studies have made progress in visualizing the internal representations within these networks, but many components of these models remain poorly understood. In contrast, language models have been more effectively internalized through the use of attention mechanisms. Building on this knowledge, a novel framework, VSFA, has been proposed to dissect deep convolutional neural networks by employing a unique hidden attention mechanism that bridges the semantic and visual domains. By treating image features and target class information as two distinct entities, VSFA offers a flexible and interpretable attention mechanism that can be easily extended to other tasks. When applied to ResNet-50, VSFA's unique attention filters demonstrate a clear relationship with specific target classes, revealing that local features grouped by column (e.g. edges, textures) or row (e.g. textures, faces) offer distinct cues, whereas the bias terms represent relative importance weights assigned by the network. Additionally, VSFA was used to develop a novel decision-making technique for evaluating and selecting specific image features relevant to each target class, supporting theories that networks prefer relevant features during training. Furthermore, VSFA enabled demonstration of class-specific feature importantency (FI) - a phenomenon where networks repeat relevant features across different instances to ensure accuracy. Both the orientation and spatial arrangements of these repeated features (i.e., PosReF) correlate with the target class, while the distribution of PosReF within the image grid influences human-like object groupings. These findings illustrate that deep neural networks employ a variety of strategies to ensure accuracy, such as repeating features and combining cues from different image features (MultMax). Importantly, VSFA's attention filters produced higher accuracy than a top model trained without attention for image classification, feature localization, and feature importance estimation tasks. Specifically, VSFA's performance surpassed the top model by 1.6% in feature localization and 3.9% in feature importance estimation. When used to recommend specific image features for a new target class, VSFA's performance exceeded that of the top model by 5.6% in feature localization and 17.2% in feature importance estimation. These results highlight the potential of VSFA to enhance computer vision models trained without attention. Furthermore, VSFA's unique attention filters can be leveraged to develop a universal image processing pipeline that generalizes across various datasets. These fluctuations result in an irregular pattern of the skyrmion lattice and a significant decrease in its melting point.
